verified_social_account.basis: The human-confirmed authoritative investor profile links directly to this account. It belongs to the Canadian investor, not the publishing author.

additional_affiliation.quote: Michael Hyatt is recognized as one of Canada’s leading tech entrepreneurs and an active investor in the technology community. He is the co-founder of BlueCat (in which Northleaf was an early investor and which was acquired by a private equity firm in 2017) and previously co-founded Dyadem (a software company that was sold to IHS in 2011).
additional_affiliation.basis: The official Northleaf appointment page explicitly identifies the same BlueCat/Dyadem co-founder.

Hello and welcome to this episode of This Is Your Life. My name is Michael Hyatt and this is the podcast dedicated to intentional leadership. My goal is to help you live with more passion, work with greater focus, and lead with extraordinary influence. In this episode, I'll be talking about the power of our own internal stories to shape how we perceive reality. In fact, these stories can covertly shape our destiny for the bad if we aren't careful, but they can also be used to shape our destiny for the good. if we're intentional change your story change your life that's what i'll cover in this episode but first this podcast is brought to you by platform university an online membership site for helping you launch your personal platform or take it to the next level you can find out more at platform university.com and i'll be telling you a little bit more about it at the end of this podcast so stay tuned so let's get right into this episode let me start with a story When I was 29 years old, I became vice president of marketing for Thomas Nelson. It was a huge step in my career. And at the time I thought I'd arrived at the pinnacle of success. I was the youngest vice president ever in the history of the company, at least as far as I knew, but I was in over my head, or at least that's the way I felt. I was just waiting for other people to come to the same conclusion. And I struggled constantly with anxiety and fear. Anxiety was kind of the daytime version and fear was the nighttime version, if you know what I mean. But this manifests itself in my body in two, frankly, embarrassing ways. First, I sweat profusely. And second, my hands were always cold. I mean, ice cold. So before attending important meetings, I would wear sometimes two t-shirts, hoping that I wouldn't sweat through both. And I strategically selected my clothing based on which colors would show the least amount of perspiration. And I would also step into the bathroom right before the meeting began and frantically run hot water over my hands and then try to dry them vigorously, praying that they would warm up before I had to meet somebody and shake hands with them. And I dreaded having to shake hands with anyone. And at some point, I realized that the problem was not in my body. But I think almost every problem we experience can be traced back to the stories that we tell ourselves. And there may be a good reason for these stories. But in the end, they produce bad outcomes if they're left unchecked. For example, I have a friend who's been unemployed now for a couple of years, and this is a person who's extremely smart, well-educated, articulate, attractive, but he's basically given up in his quest to find a job. Everyone I get close to eventually leaves me. And guess what? That's exactly what happens because she believes her story. And there are lots of people like Gail and I who want to be around her and enjoy her company. But she discounts that kind of evidence. Why? Because of the story she's allowing to play in the theater of her mind. The bottom line is that you don't have to be controlled by bad stories. You can take control of them. You can change your life by changing your story. And I'd like to suggest five ways to take control of the narrative in your head. Number 1 recognize the voice in your head. You have to realize that this voice is not you. It pretends to be you. It might even sound like you. It probably, in fact, does sound like you. It talks to you in your own voice, but it's not. Maybe it's coming from your parents. Maybe it's coming from a teacher or an abusive spouse. It doesn't matter. Just recognize that it's happening. All you're trying to do in this stage is become aware that there's a narrator and he's telling you how things are, or at least how he perceives them to be and what you need to believe about reality. So recognize the voice that's in your head. Number two. Jot down what the voice is saying. This can be really helpful. It might be something like, I'm too young, or I'm too old, or I'm not very well educated, or I'm overeducated, or I don't have enough experience, or I don't have the right experience, or I can't write, or I always quit, or I'm not creative, or I always eventually fail, or I'm not very good with money. Jeremy, in my experience, what gets scheduled gets done. And so put it on your calendar. I don't think it has to take an enormous amount of time. I spend about 30 minutes a day on Twitter, and I talk about that in the book platform. about how to be really efficient and how to become a Twitter ninja in 30 minutes a day or less. In terms of blogging, that may take a little bit longer. I wrote for years just doing two or three posts a week, and those would typically take me anywhere from 60 to 70 minutes per post. And you do get better and faster over time. So I would just encourage you to schedule that. I used to write late at night because that was the only time I had. I was a very busy CEO, and my company had the first of my time, and my family also had my time. So this had to come in third place. And so I would just, again, encourage you to schedule it and work from there and make sure that you're disciplined in it. Next question from J.D. Smith.

[SPEAKER_02]
Michael Hyatt, this is J.D. Smith in Charlotte, North Carolina at cityimpact.org. Michael, what are the best three ways to... separate and yet keep intersected the platforms of a business or ministry. and the founders of that business or ministry as things multiply and grow forward. Thanks and look forward to hearing your answer. God bless.

[SPEAKER_01]
J.D., I don't know if I can come up with three ways, but I would say this, and it's kind of back to the question that I think Sarah asked earlier, and that is people connect with people. They don't connect with organizations. They don't connect with businesses primarily. You just look back when I was the CEO of Thomas Nelson, and I had probably 10 times the number of Twitter followers as the Thomas Nelson Twitter account did. And again, for the very same reason, when you follow a business on Twitter or on Facebook, you expect them to be promoting to you. And if you're interested in the product, great, but you can only handle so much of that. Again, you're going to be so much more connected to the individuals. So I would encourage the founders, the CEOs, the leadership of the company or the ministry or the organization to Twitter under their own names, to do Facebook under their own names. Do it as an organization too, but try to get as many links, I guess, or tentacles out there into the marketplace to try to bring people into your business. It's all good. The benefit of the company will accrue to the individuals, and conversely, the brand equity in the individuals will accrue to the company. So I do not make a hard, fast line between those two. Everybody is an ambassador for the company or the organization, and the organization ought to be serving the individuals into it. So I think if you'll just let it flow organically, it'll all be good. Next question from Tom Schulte.

[SPEAKER_06]
Hi Michael, this is Tom Schulte calling from Atlanta, Georgia with the Link to Leadership group. I have a popular group on LinkedIn with 22,000 members called Link to Leadership and a blog, also at linktoleadership.com, that gets about 25,000 page views per month. My question is, how do I move this group from an embassy site, which is LinkedIn, over to a home-based or self-hosted community? I'd love to hear your thoughts. Thanks.

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, first of all, Tom, good for you to be able to recognize the difference between a home base and an embassy. There really is a difference. And for those of you who haven't read the book, obviously Tom has. Let me just articulate those quickly or the differences. A home base is a place in cyberspace that you own and control. That's the key thing. You have total control over the messaging. You have total control over the branding. And this is your home base. It's the place that you refer everyone else to. It could be a podcast. It could be a blog. It could be a website. It could be a video site. But again, the emphasis is on ownership and control. In my case, michaelhyatt.com is my home base. I get involved in these embassies out there like Facebook, Twitter, Google+, Pinterest, all the other social networking sites. But I use those as a way to go to where the people are, to engage them there, and then to refer them back to my home base. Because I really don't know if those embassies, again, a place where you need credentials and you have a presence, but you don't own. You never know how long those are going to be around or if they're going to change or if you're going to continue to be able to find your best customers and your fans there. So, again, I see them as embassies. Well, what happens in the case of Tom where you've built essentially a home base in what is an embassy site, a place that you don't control or don't own? I think my recommendation, Tom, would be to go ahead and build out your home base on self-hosted WordPress. I mean, you use that term, so I assume you know what that is. But for the rest of you that don't, first of all, don't get hung up on it. It basically means where you install WordPress on a server that you're either leasing or renting or controlling and have your presence there. But the thing I would say, Tom, is go ahead and establish your home base there. I think I would duplicate the content for a while at least on LinkedIn, but constantly refer people back to your home base. Tell them you're moving things there, that you'll continue to have a presence on LinkedIn, but you're going to move it to your own site. where you have more control over the content and you're able to add some additional features that will benefit the people that follow you. And that's how I would always couch it, how I would always position it or present it to the people that are part of your group. And that is you're doing it for them, not just for yourself, but this is going to be a better experience for them. And I would give it some time. Again, I would probably duplicate the content for a while before I would move exclusively over to your own site because you're going to lose some people if you just move it abruptly. The next question comes from Wanda Ball.

[SPEAKER_12]
Hi, Michael. My name is Wanda Ball, and I am from Chino, California. I am the author and publisher of ballpublications.com. I currently speak at my local church, and I have now decided to... become a public speaker. I want to broaden my platform. So I wanted to know, how do I actually market myself to a broader audience? Thank you.

[SPEAKER_01]
One of the first thing I would suggest is you've got to get a speaker's page on your blog or on your website. And the person that you need to be thinking about as you're developing that speaker's page is the event planner, because people who are shopping for speakers are looking for specific things they want. For example, they want to see what other people are saying about your speaking. So begin getting endorsements. from the events where you've spoken and those may be sparse initially, but go ahead and get them anyway. And then a standard operating procedure, always get them immediately after you speak for an event planner. I would also put a video of you speaking on there. That's probably the most important thing. that event planners look for is they want to see you in action. They want to know, you know, can you deliver the bacon when you're in front of an audience? So that's key as well. A list of your topics. What are your two or three top topics, the most requested topics that people are looking for? And then your schedule of speaking events. And I have a list of these in the book, Platform, Get Noticed in a Noisy World, all the elements that make up for a dynamic speaking page and I would encourage you to replicate that Then what I would do is try to get that landing page, the link to that landing page out in your social media networks. You can't overdo it. In other words, I should say you can overdo it. Don't do it too much. Don't be so promotional that you're just constantly spamming your followers, pushing your own speaking. I do it occasionally, but not that often. If you start delivering quality content or if you are delivering quality content via your blog or podcasting or video or some other mechanism, you're going to create demand. People are going to want more of you. They're going to want to hear you speak, and it will develop organically. But start by creating a place, a home for your speaking, where people can go and get information. Until you have a landing page, essentially you're not in business as a speaker. So I would start there. Next question comes from Joshua Bedford.

[SPEAKER_10]
Hey, Michael. My name is Joshua Bedford, and I'm from Mississippi. My website and blog can be found at joshuabedford.com. In your section on Twitter, you advise to automate our delivery of tweets. This probably depends on the number of tweets, but how long do you suggest we space them apart?

[SPEAKER_01]
Joshua, I think that's a highly individual question, and you're probably going to just have to experiment to find the right rhythm, the right frequency, the right volume of tweets. It's very much different on Twitter than it is on Facebook. I found on Facebook that I can do about two status updates a day, and that's about all anybody wants to hear from me. I mean, it's just an environment or a culture on Facebook that is not conducive to multiple updates per day. Now, some people misuse Facebook, and I think they suffer the consequences of that, and I did that initially too. In fact, I was initially just feeding my tweets into Facebook, but it overwhelmed the people who are trying to follow me on Facebook, and I didn't get much traction there until I changed my strategy. I would say, though, that on Twitter, and that's the question you ask about, on Twitter, this is for me, and this is what I found over time, but I do about 13 to 15 updates per day. Now, I space those out using Buffer. It's a little application that enables me to load the tweets on the front end. And I do this in about 30 minutes at the beginning of the day. as I'm going through my RSS feeds, as I'm going through email newsletters that I get, as I'm searching other web content, I find links that I think are gonna be interesting and useful to my followers. And I post a status update for Twitter in Buffer and then Buffer spreads them throughout the day. And I try to do these about one an hour. And I avoid times like, you know, at the end of the day, between about five and seven, typically when people are in a commute and not paying attention. But again, for me, it works about once per hour. Again, if it's more than that, I get some fall off because people just say it's just too much. If it's less than that, you know, people want more and I hear from them, but I've just, you know, figured this out over time. So again, for me, it's about once an hour, your mileage may vary. Next question.

[SPEAKER_00]
comes from Paul Evans. Hi, Michael. Paul Evans calling from Montgomery, Alabama. My website is paulbevans.com. How bold do you need to be when you're wanting to expand your platform? You're really wanting people to take your message to... share it to tell others about it, tweet about it, comment, etc. How bold can you actually be? I've noticed that some people don't always take the initiative. So what are some suggestions you have to encourage other people to share your message for you?

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, I don't guess I really believe in asking directly too much. In other words, I would never DM somebody on Twitter or Facebook them or send them an email and say, hey, can you spread this message? I mean, it's very rare for me to do that. I shouldn't say I wouldn't ever do it or I haven't ever done it because I have. But it's very rare. I think you can really wear out people and put them in an awkward position. If your content is great, they're going to want to share it. You're not going to have to talk them into it or beg for it. I can tell you the people that asked me to retweet stuff on Twitter, I almost never retweet it. I think to myself, if you have to ask me, you're not creating wow content to begin with. And again, that's not a hard, fast rule, but I usually think if somebody's asking, you know, there's something up there that makes me suspicious. Now, having said that, I would have a clear mechanism on my blog that enables people to share the content if they find it engaging. So to have social media buttons or some other way to share it on Facebook, a like button or a Twitter button, man, if you go to my website at michaelhyatt.com, you will find those things front and center. Well, actually top and center. But with every blog post, there is a mechanism for sharing it and people use those like crazy. And it's one of the reasons I get so much engagement, the social proof at the top, that talks about how many comments, how many, you know, Facebook shares, how many tweets, those are all important for creating authority for the post or social validation for the post. But it also creates a mechanism for them to share it with their followers, which is the key to amplification and creating traffic. Next question comes from Rebecca Livermore.

[SPEAKER_04]
Hi Michael, this is Rebecca Livermore from ProfessionalContentCreation.com. And the question that I have for you is what is the best way for people who are introverts who maybe don't like... getting up in front of people speaking or going to live events and networking. to build a platform. Thanks so much!

[SPEAKER_01]
Rebecca, there's a lot that I could share about this. Let me just say to begin with that I am an introvert myself. I am very introverted. I'm naturally shy in a group of people. I kind of keep to myself. I don't draw energy from people. But over time, I've learned to kind of, you know, turn it on, hopefully in a genuine and authentic way. But the way I do that is I make it about the other person. I try to be really naturally inquisitive so that if I'm in a room of people trying to network, I'm not there self-promoting. I don't do that very well. But I love to ask questions and find out more about other people. And as it turns out, other people's favorite topic, their favorite subject to talk about is, guess what? Themselves. That's right. So I think if you make it about that, it will help you to focus less on yourself, more about them, and put you at ease. Having said that, I do think that you're going to have to put yourself out there. You know, if you're going to build a platform, you're going to have to move outside of your current comfort zone. And the thing that I would say there is that the solution to your current problem, and I've said this in many contexts, is outside of your comfort zone. That's where growth occurs. You have to be willing to move outside of your comfort zone if you're going to grow. If you're not willing to do that, you're not going to grow a platform. And frankly, you're probably not going to accomplish a whole lot. So you've got to be willing to be brave, to be courageous, and to step out a little bit in order to build a platform. Next question comes from Jane Graham.

[SPEAKER_03]
Hi Michael, my name is Jane Graham. I'm calling from West Michigan and I blog about faith at girlmeetspaper.com. I'm just wondering if you can offer some insight to this little dilemma. You talked about in your last podcast how it's the people who stick with it who will kind of overcome that pinnacle and see their blog take off. And if you just hang in there and persevere that perhaps you're on the brink of something big and you don't even know it, and if you give up and walk away, you'd lose that great experience. At the same time, I've heard other bloggers who are really successful and who I respect. talk about how they had to make the tough decision to scrap an old blog and start over and how they've finally gained the traction that they had been looking for in doing so. So I'm just wondering, how do you know if you're on the wrong track? How do you know if your message is just boring or you're just a bad writer or when it's just a growth issue and it just takes time? So I'm having trouble discerning between the two and I'd love your thoughts. Thanks so much.

[SPEAKER_01]
Gene, that's a great question. And I would encourage you to read Seth Godin's book, The Dip. where he answers that. It's a very short book. You can read through it, but he answers the question, when do you know to give up and go to something else or persevere through the dip and see the upside on the other side? So that's a great book to start with. I would say just because I say to stick with it and persevere doesn't mean that you have to beat a dead horse or stay with the same concept. You can switch that. When I started blogging in 2004, my blog was called Working Smart and I blogged almost exclusively on productivity. But after a while, I started running out of things to say and it just didn't interest me. It didn't fire up my imagination and I wanted to move on to something else. So I started, I kind of redesigned the blog. I renamed it still under michaelhyatt.com, but I called it From Where I Sit and my intention was to blog as a new CEO and to blog as a publishing executive and kind of pull the curtain apart and let people see into the mysterious world of publishing. But after a while, that also kind of ran its course and I started to see a decrease in my traffic and so I kind of reinvented myself for the third time. And then I decided I was gonna just write on leadership and social media and still publishing and still productivity, but I was gonna broaden it a little bit. My point is that just because I was committed to persevering and succeeding, as it was in the start of this world you like been designated, didn't mean I was committed to running a concept that had sort of, you know, it had outlasted its life. I think you've got to be discerning about that. And one of the things I look for is comments, not volume, but the quality of comments. What are people telling me? Are they finding my content helpful? Is it adding value? If I'm not getting any of that, then I probably would seriously question about whether I'm on the right track or not. So hope that's helpful. Next question is from Casey Kupp.

[SPEAKER_09]
Hi Michael, my name is KC Cup and I'm calling from Rock Island, Illinois. I blog at KCcup.com. My question today is, what is a good balance for promoting your blog or product so you don't come across as narcissistic and self-absorbed? You do a wonderful job with this, so I'm definitely looking forward to hearing your wisdom in this area. Thanks, Michael. Keep up the great work.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thanks, Casey. I would say that generosity should be your guide. I've got a whole chapter on this in the book platform. It's called the 20 to 1, 20 to 1 rule. And it's all about the number of deposits that you make versus the withdrawals you make from your audience. And I don't know if the ratio is exactly right, but you've got to make a lot more deposits. You've got to add a lot of value before you start extracting value. So again, I try about one out of 20 posts. This week, last week has been a little crazy because I was promoting my book. But normally I'm really trying to add value and make sure that I'm pointing people to other resources and things that are going to help them as opposed to pointing them to my resources and kind of tooting my own horn. So I hope that'll be helpful. And I would read that chapter in the book. I think it will help you further. Next question is from Tammy Helfrich.

[SPEAKER_08]
Hi Michael, it's Tammy Helfrich. I blog at TammyHelfrich.wordpress.com. My question is, when do you think is the optimum time to start putting advertising on your blog? What do you think that most advertisers would look for? before even considering paying to be a part of your blog. Thanks so much.

[SPEAKER_01]
I think you need about 10,000 unique visitors a month before it starts making sense for advertisers to go to the hassle of signing up to run advertising on your blog. Now, you can use Google AdWords and some other networks with less volume than that, but I just wonder if it's really worth it. I waited until I had about 20,000 plus unique visitors a month before I started monetizing my blog through advertising. And your mileage may vary on that as well. You can be experimental on it and just see, but the thing you don't want to do is launch an advertising offering to the marketplace and then have nobody sign up and you've got all these blank spots on your blog. So I would start with fewer spots, advertising spots, and I would do what I could to make those sell out initially. And I'll tell you when I started, and I don't even think I talk about this in the book, but when I started, I gave away those spots. I contacted some of my friends who had products or services that I thought would have affinity for my audience. And I said, hey, I'm about to start advertising on my site. How about if I just give you a free slot here for a month and just see how it goes and you can kind of tell me about your experience? Well, that kind of created the impression that my spots were in demand and that people were clamoring for them. And then the next month, people started paying for them a little bit at a time, and I started giving those free slots up and letting one slot be available so that I could sell it. But again, I think probably the right level is about 10,000 unique visitors a month before you start to consider it. The last question, we're about out of time, comes from Kelly Combs.

[SPEAKER_05]
It's Kelly Combs from Virginia at KellyCombs.com. Michael, I love in your book platform that you say, be generous. And if you want to build a social media platform, that you have to be a giver and not a taker. I see you act this out. by having guest bloggers. and sharing your platform with them and the giveaways you have on your blog. But my question is, if you don't already have a large platform or products to give away, what are some examples of ways we can be generous?

[SPEAKER_01]
This is also a great question, Kelly. And just the fact that you're asking this question shows that you're headed in the right direction because generosity is the best marketing strategy that you could ever use. One of the things that I found as I was out kind of foraging on the internet looking for resources for my audience of readers is that that was one of the things that I could offer. And it was not only something that I was offering to my readers, but something that I was offering to these other bloggers was exposure to my audience. So I think at the very least, do that. You can also offer links on your blog to other bloggers so that they get some exposure and some backlinks there. I think also commenting on other blogs is a great way to create engagement on those blogs. And again, to give you backlinks. So any way you can be generous, any way you can give to others is a great way for you to succeed and to gain some. credibility with those other bloggers, which eventually, if you're going to build a platform, if you've got something you're going to sell eventually or message you're trying to promote, you're going to need that. And it paid off for me this last week in spades because for years, I've been giving to other bloggers and I've been pointing my resources to other people and trying to help them when they would write a book or whatever. And then it came time for them to do that for me this last week. And oh my gosh, I was just overwhelmed with the generosity of my friends and the people that I'd met on cyberspace. So that's about it. That's about all the time we have for questions. I think that was a record. We got in a number of questions, more than I've ever done before. I hope that was helpful to you. Again, the book is called Platform, Get Noticed in a Noisy World. Please tell your friends about this book. If you haven't, you can find more details at platformbook.com. Next week, I'm going to be at Blog World and the New Media Expo in New York City. I've got a private event I'm doing on Monday, and then I'll be up at Blog World on Tuesday through Thursday. And I'm going to be speaking at one of the super sessions on Thursday morning, June the 7th at 9 a.m. And I'm going to be speaking on the subject of platform and especially how I'm applying it to my new podcast and what I've been learning and building a platform in the podcast space, which, oh my gosh, it's been like a whole brand new experience for me. But you can get more information at michaelhyatt.com forward slash blog world. Well, that's about it for this episode of This Is Your Life. In the next episode, I want to talk about, back to leadership topic, I want to talk about how to create alignment in teams. So if you have a question about this topic, about creating organizational alignment. alignment in your team you can leave a voicemail for me at michaelhyatt.com forward slash podcast question. And if you want to leave a comment on this podcast, You can do so at michaelhyatt.com forward slash 014 as in episode 14. michaelhyatt.com forward slash 014. I'd also be grateful if you'd rate my podcast on iTunes. That helps me tremendously with keeping my podcast visible so people who have never heard of it can discover it. So until next time, remember, your life is a gift. Now go make it count.

[SPEAKER_00]
This is your life Are you who you wanna be?

[SPEAKER_03]
Hello and welcome to another episode of This Is Your Life. My name is Michael Hyatt and this is the podcast dedicated to intentional leadership. My goal is to help you live with more passion, work with greater focus, and lead with extraordinary influence. In this episode, we're going to be talking about organizational alignment, one of my favorite topics, and I'm going to share with you three key disciplines that you must practice in order to achieve it and maintain it. And I don't care if the context of your leadership is your family, your small business, a large corporation, a network of freelancers or volunteers, or a church or ministry, you need to know these three disciplines and practice them faithfully if you're going to be successful. But first, this podcast is brought to you by Dynamic Communicators International, producers of the SCORE, Launch, and Platform conferences. These unique events are designed for professional speakers and those who simply want to communicate more professionally. You can find out more information at dynamiccommunicators.com. So let's talk about alignment. In my experience, weak leaders blame their followers for a lack of alignment. Strong leaders, on the other hand, know that it's their responsibility to create it. Alignment is not one of those things that just happens. It's created. That's an important distinction, I think, for you to make in your own mind. But years ago, I was making a major presentation to a prospective author back when I was just beginning in the publishing business. And my boss was there, as was my boss's boss or the big boss. But our goal was to sign the author and win his business. And everyone on our team was nervous, especially me, since I was the one doing the presenting. And it was one of my first major presentations in front of a bestselling author that we were trying to acquire for our publishing company. But prior to that meeting, I had shared my presentation. It was a nicely bound presentation. It had slides and the whole nine yards. But I shared it with my boss. He reviewed it carefully. He offered some really helpful feedback. And once we were both happy with it, he shared it with the big boss. And the big boss didn't comment. So we both assumed he was fine with it. And as it turns out, that was kind of his typical MO. But as I was actually making the presentation, I could tell that the big boss was uncomfortable. You know, just the way he looked. I don't know. I just sensed it in the air. But he didn't say anything. But he was visibly agitated. And I just sensed that we weren't aligned. But he remained quiet. So after the presentation, the prospective author asked me several direct questions. And I provided what I thought were simple and honest answers. And my immediate boss who was there chimed in a few times to agree or just to amplify on what I'd already said. But the author seemed satisfied. And in fact, he gave us permission to proceed with the contract. In other words, it was pretty much a done deal. But he expressed his enthusiasm about doing business together. And, you know, we shook hands. And we flew out. We left. But I was proud of the outcome. And my boss was happy about it. And we moved on to the next thing. And I think the big boss flew from there somewhere else. So we didn't see him immediately after that meeting. And I think the big boss was happy about it. But a few days after the meeting, the big boss sends me a blistering memo. And this was back in the days before email. I know it's hard to imagine, but there was a time when there was no such thing as email. But he copied my boss and sent it directly to me. And the bottom line was he wasn't happy with the financial arrangement that I had proposed at the meeting. And he challenged my motives even, going so far as to ask if I was somehow in alliance with the other side. And it really, really hurt me. In fact, it was demoralizing and I almost quit my job as a result of it. But here's what I got from that looking back. And although it was painful at the time, the experience was very instructive, particularly about this issue of alignment. As a leader, I'm responsible for creating organizational alignment with my team. So if something slips out of alignment and I'm unhappy with the outcome, then I've got to ask a very important question. And that is this. What was it about my leadership that created this outcome? I want to tell you, if you want to grow in your leadership, this is a critically important question. A question you should be asking yourself constantly as things happen in your organization. What was it about my leadership that created this outcome? By the way, that's both positive and negative. You can take credit for the things that happen that are good. But you've got to take full responsibility when things don't turn out how you intended. And this is something I'm sure that the big boss in my story example never asked himself. He was just in blame mode. Instead of asking himself, what was it that he didn't do? And despite the fact that he had a chance to weigh in in the preparation before we made the presentation, he didn't do it. And then when things didn't go like he wanted, he got upset. And I was not that pleased either, frankly, with his response. But as a leader, you can create alignment in your team by practicing three key disciplines. And again, I just want to remind you that this is not just for people who are leading large businesses. It works in small business. It works with freelancers and volunteers. It works in the ministry. I spent six years in the ministry. So I've been in that situation. It works in your family. Anywhere you're trying to create alignment, you need to practice these three disciplines. So discipline number one is the discipline of contact. Now look, alignment is not an event. It's a process. Teams go in and out of alignment. It's not like you just accomplish it once and then you can check it off your to-do list and you're done with alignment. No. Teams go in and out of alignment. And keeping your team aligned takes work. It takes constant work. And you're not going to keep your team aligned unless you have frequent contact with them. And that's what I mean by the discipline of contact. And that's what I mean by the discipline of contact. they're going to do the best they can with what you give them. So if you don't spend time with them, it's inevitable that they're going to make decisions that you're uncomfortable with. And that's essentially what happened in the story that I told about the big boss. He had an opportunity to weigh in. He could have met with me before the meeting, which by the way, I would always urge you to do when you've got a big presentation is meet with your team, make sure everybody's in alignment before you go on the field and play the game as it were. But he didn't do that. And if you don't spend time with people, again, it's inevitable. They're going to make decisions you're uncomfortable with. But here's the thing. It's your responsibility to initiate this contact. You're the leader. You're leading the team. You're the quarterback on the field. It's your job to initiate this contact. And you can do this in a variety of ways. You can do it in your regular one-on-one meetings, staff meetings, just by walking around. But it's the discipline of contact. The second discipline. It's what I would call the discipline of communication. Contact is not enough. You've got to communicate. Okay, this is obvious, but I meet a lot of leaders that act as though this weren't true. People cannot read your mind. They need to know what you expect. They need to understand your expectations. What are the outcomes that you're trying to produce in this project or with these goals or with this particular cause or whatever it is? They need to understand explicitly what your expectations are. They also need to understand overall the organization's mission and vision. You need to verbalize it over and over and over and over again. You cannot speak the vision too much. Andy Stanley says that vision leaks, and I think he's exactly right. You've got to keep filling up the bucket, the vision bucket, over and over again because your people forget it. They get so caught up in the daily activity of the organization that they forget about the vision. They get disoriented. They get organizational vertigo. And your job as a leader is to keep speaking into that the vision that keeps them connected to the larger picture. Somebody once told me, and I think this is right, is talk until you're sick of hearing yourself talk about the vision and you're about half done. In other words, double it. Talk till you're sick of hearing yourself talk about the vision and really you've only just begun. Double it and keep talking about it. And here's the thing, if you don't like something, you need to speak up before you get into a high stakes situation where dialogue is happening in real time. And if something sneaks out that you weren't prepared for or one of your people says something because you weren't prepared or didn't discuss it, own it. You can have a constructive conversation with them after the fact. And maybe they were out of line or they were naive or they were overstepping their bounds. But you can talk about that after the fact in a creative conversation or a creative criticism conversation. But it's not really fair to them or to you to do this after the fact and second guess their motives and judge them essentially for something you didn't do on the front end, which was to create alignment. That's your job as the leader. Discipline number three. is the discipline of connection. Communication is not even enough. Yeah, you've got to have the discipline of contact. You've got to have the discipline of communication. but you must practice the discipline of connection. Listen to this. For true alignment to take place, your people have got to know and trust. your heart. They got to know and trust your heart. They got to be committed to your success and the success of the team. And you may be tempted to think that you're entitled to their full engagement by virtue of you employing them. You're not. You can buy their presence, but you can't buy their heart. you've got to earn it people will show up they'll go through the motions they'll nod when they're supposed to nod they'll say what they're supposed to say but that's way way different than having true commitment that comes from the heart and alignment is one of those things that has to come from the heart you're not just after agreement You're after alignment, which is a very different thing. And I would just urge you to consider the distinction between those two things. We get in meetings sometimes and people agree, but they really haven't bought into the vision. They haven't bought into the project. They're not aligned. In other words, they're not willing to exert their blood, sweat, and tears to make it happen. They're not willing to take a bullet for the team because they're not aligned. They may be in agreement. They're just not committed from the heart level. So you've got to have the commitment or the buy-in at the heart level. And you can only create a connection and thus alignment when you open your heart and letter the people in. And I find one of the best ways to do this is to talk about the why. And you've heard me say this on this podcast. And if you've been reading my blog, you know that I say this a lot. When people lose their why, they lose their way. It's really easy to do. People forget what's at stake. They forget why they're doing something. I remember one time at Thomas Nelson, this may have been 2007, 2008, we had a very audacious goal for that year. And rather than talking about it in corporate speak, I got the executive team together, and actually this was about 50 or 60 of our vice presidents. We got them together. And I just talked about the why, why it was important that we accomplish this goal. And honestly, it had very little to do with the finances. I mean, certainly we expressed it in terms of a financial goal, but that was just a number. It was really about us growing as a team, accomplishing something significant in terms of making a dent in the universe and making an impact on our industry. It was really about us being able to earn bonuses for our entire team so that people would be able to do the things that they dreamed about financially as families. And I just talked like that. I just talked about the why of why we were pursuing this goal and why it mattered, because I wanted to connect with them. It wasn't manipulation. It was heartfelt. And I meant every word of it. So three disciplines, the discipline of contact. the discipline of communication, and the discipline of connection. Alignment is critical if you want to get the right things done and move your organization forward in the most effective and efficient way possible. And it's not something that's going to happen on its own. As a leader, you've got to take the initiative to create it. So let me ask you this question. Is your team aligned? Think about the project that you're working on right now, the major initiative that you've taken on as a team. Is your team aligned? What can you do today to create that alignment? If you want to comment on this episode, please go to my blog at michaelhyatt.com forward slash 015, as in episode 15, michaelhyatt.com forward slash 015. I had a few questions come in on this topic when I posted them on Twitter and when I mentioned at the end of the podcast last week. So I want to take those. I had the first question from Nick Cook. Take it away, Nick.

Hi, Michael. My name is Nick Cook calling from Columbus, Ohio. I'm just getting started blogging. in building a personal platform. at what the world neglects. dot com Michael, my question for you in terms of aligning teams with this is, What were some of the primary... personal growth, Um, areas you had to improve in. Or some of the primary ways you had to change. in your journey from being a beginning leader to being an experienced leader. when it comes to aligning teams. I'm personally a young leader. And I had to learn that we created the vision most effectively when we created it together. So I had to blow off efficiency in one sense, in order or for the sake of ownership. in a very real sense. So I had to learn to get the team together and create the vision together so that we had ownership in the vision. Another thing I had to learn as a young leader was to keep speaking the vision. And I'll tell you, I haven't always done this well. There have been times that I forget to speak it or frankly, I get tired of hearing it myself. So I think that everybody else is tired of it, but they're not getting tired of it. They're not getting tired of it because they're getting the vision beat out of them on the battlefield as they're encountering day-to-day problems. So you have to keep speaking it, as I already said. I think you also have to keep calling people to the vision and calling them to step up and perform. And this was not easy either because I felt like maybe that I was pushing a little bit too much or that I was being a little too aggressive, but I learned that people will step up when you expect them to step up, when you call them to step up. And I can think of one meeting in particular that we had where we were very close. It was in August, I don't know, maybe about seven or eight years ago. It was in August when it was a very big month for us. We were shipping into the fall selling season, preparing for Christmas. And it looked like we were going to miss the month by a couple million dollars because we couldn't get the orders out of the warehouse. And I remember sitting in an executive committee meeting and asking our distribution manager, I said, what would it take to make this possible? Failure is not an option, you know, to steal a line from Apollo 13. Failure is not an option. We've got to get these orders out the door. We committed to the board. We committed to ourselves. We've got to stand for this and make it happen. And it was amazing to see what happened just by asking that question because the guy that was running that business, running the distribution business, wanted to be a hero. He stepped up, his people made it happen, and it was awesome. But it was because I asked the question and it was outside of my comfort zone. And as I've said on this podcast before, most of the solutions to your problems are outside of your comfort zone. But I was willing to step out there. And it's not always easy, but it's always important. By the way, another thing that I went through in terms of training that was enormously helpful to me in terms of learning about alignment, I took my whole team through a course put on by Gap International called the Alignment Intensive. It was phenomenal. It was about a week long. It was in Philadelphia. And I'll have a link in the show notes to where you can get more information about this. But it's not cheap, but it is great because we all worked on it together. It gave us a common language to talk about alignment. And we began to work on some real-life problems in the context of that seminar, along with about 80 other people from all kinds of different industries. BMO reaffirms commitment as the bank for business with content focused on business resiliency and growth to help clients make real financial progress

Well-known entrepreneur and investor

Michael Hyatt

headlines as the host of the podcast

TORONTO

,

June 25, 2020

/CNW/ - BMO has today introduced a new podcast dedicated to Canadian businesses. The podcast –

Business Unplanned

– will provide business owners with expert opinions and advice on business resiliency and adaptability during this uncertain time. This announcement builds off of the bank's recently introduced

online resource hub

and will provide Canadian businesses with an additional resource to help their long-term growth.

"We are helping thousands of businesses across geographies and sectors every week and are constantly looking for opportunities to do more," said

Erminia (Ernie) Johannson

, Group Head, North American Personal and Business Banking, BMO Financial Group. "In conversations with our clients, we heard how important and beneficial it is for them to have a community where they can learn from each other. We have now created an additional resource where businesses can come together and learn from entrepreneurs and business owners and apply best practices to their own businesses."

Business Unplanned

will feature six episodes and be available on

bmo.com/BusinessUnplanned

as well as on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and Google Podcasts. Episodes will be released periodically throughout the summer. Entrepreneur, investor, and co-founder of BlueCat,

Michael Hyatt

, has joined as the host of

Business Unplanned

. He will lead listeners on a journey as they dive into stories from leading entrepreneurs and small business owners.

"More than ever before, leaders need to come together to help both small businesses and the wider business community overcome the challenges of this pandemic," said Mr. Hyatt. "Joining BMO as the host of Business Unplanned is a way to do that and provides an outlet where business owners can relate to what we are sharing and take away actionable advice for their business."

The podcast will include guests from a range of sectors and business size and will cover:

Episode 1: The Business Recovery

Episode 2: Making Business Adjustments: How to Plan Post-Pandemic

Episode 3: Getting a Business Loan During Covid-19

Episode 4: Managing Cash Flow Post-Covid-19

Episode 5: How to Stay Motivated in Business

Episode 6: Understanding Customers' Needs

To access BMO's Business Resource Hub, visit:

https://www.bmo.com/main/business/small-business-resource-hub/

.

To stay connected with BMO or to access the bank's new online support tool, visit:

bmo.com/covid19

.

About BMO Financial Group

Serving customers for 200 years and counting, BMO is a highly diversified financial services provider - the 8th largest bank, by assets, in North America. With total assets of $987 billion as of April 30, 2020, and a team of diverse and highly engaged employees, BMO provides a broad range of personal and commercial banking, wealth management and investment banking products and services to more than 12 million customers and conducts business through three operating groups: Personal and Commercial Banking, BMO Wealth Management and BMO Capital Markets.

Area of Expertise

Vanessa

is a Senior Counsel at RBC. Prior to joining RBC, Vanessa was a litigation counsel at the Department of Justice Canada, specializing in a broad range of complex legal and policy matters involving social benefits programs and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Vanessa regularly represented the Attorney General of Canada before the Federal Court and the Federal Court of Appeal.

Vanessa is on the Board of Directors of International Planned Parenthood Federation / Western Hemisphere Region and of IPPF Canada. She was a guest speaker on women empowerment at the International Women’s Empowerment and Leadership Conference and at the Women’s Festival Toronto Gala. She has volunteered for the Elizabeth Fry Society of Ottawa, which supports and advocates for young and adult women who are criminalized or may become criminalized. She earned both a JD and a License of Civil Law from the University of Ottawa. Vanessa speaks English, French and Spanish fluently.

Michael

Hyatt is the co-founder of BlueCat, which was sold to Madison Dearborn Partners, of Chicago, IL. He serves as a director of BlueCat, ranks as one of Canada’s top entrepreneurs, and is known as a technology visionary. Michael is also a weekly business commentator on CBC and was a celebrated “Dragon” on CBC’s online Dragons’ Den. He is the Host of BMO’s Unplanned Business podcast to help small businesses and an investor on the hit Spotify podcast “The Pitch”. Michael is a Founding Partner and Fellow at the Rotman School of Management’s prestigious Creative Destruction Lab and sits on the CEO Board of Advisors of Georgian Partners, one of Canada’s leading venture capital firms. He was also recently named Entrepreneur in Residence (EIR) at Blakes, one of the most successful law firms in the country.

Michael was awarded the “Power Partner Award” from the Women of Inspiration Awards for his supportive and innovative work with Women in Canada and the developing world.

Michael and Vanessa

are active investors and philanthropists who are part of the Hyatt Family Foundation. The foundation focuses on women’s health, critical hospital research and sponsorship of underprivileged minorities.

BlueCat Networks, a Toronto-based provider of enterprise-class IP Address Management (IPAM) platforms, has raised a $11m first equity financing.

The round was led by Bridgescale Partners, a California-based investment firm providing equity to high growth information technology companies.

As stated by Michael Hyatt, CEO and co-founder of the company, whose IP Address Management (IPAM) platforms as well as Domain Name System (DNS) and Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) solutions have been deployed to meet the rising IP management demands of government, military and both medium and large enterprises worldwide, BlueCat Networks will use the proceeds to further enhance its product line and continue the rapid expansion of its global distribution network.

Successful entrepreneurs often make unsuccessful investors when they sell their companies and become full-time family office chiefs instead, according to a leading family office founder. "It's humbling," said Michael Hyatt, a software entrepreneur and principal of the Hyatt Family Office. "You need to fall on your face and realize that if you're a great entrepreneur, you're likely a pretty bad investor. Start with that, admit you're not good. And you can probably do some good things." Hyatt, 48, co-founded and sold two software companies — Dyadem and BlueCat Networks — before launching the Hyatt Family Office in 2017. A self-made millionaire by the age of 25, Hyatt sold BlueCat for $400 million in 2017. While he declined to comment on the size of the Hyatt Family Office, industry experts estimate its current assets at between $400 million to $600 million. (See the full special interview with Hyatt above.) The rapid growth of family offices — which now number as many as 10,000 worldwide, according to EY — is being driven in large part by entrepreneurs who have sold their companies or taken them public, creating massive liquidity. While older family offices were largely built on inherited wealth and highly conservative investing philosophies, a new generation of family offices is run by born risk-takers who aim for exponential returns -- traits that sometimes also make for costly mistakes. "To be an entrepreneur, you have to be a risk-taker, Machiavellian, damn the torpedoes," Hyatt said. "If you actually calculated the risks of building and exiting a company for, say, over $1 billion, you probably never would have started the company. But when you have money, you have to go from wealth creation to wealth preservation. And that's an entirely different ballgame. It's not sexy. It's boring and you have to save yourself from yourself." Sobering juice bankruptcy Hyatt said that one of his early family office investments was in a juice start-up. He studied the numbers, got to the know the founder and did deep information dives on the juice business before investing. Other sophisticated investors were also buying in. The company went bankrupt less than a year after he invested. Today, the Hyatt Family Office has a diversified portfolio, aiming for a third of its assets to be invested in stocks, a third in real estate and a third in venture capital and private equity. His goal is returns of 8% a year. "We don't push the boundaries," he said. "I've had outcomes where I feel like a genius but I realized I took way too much risk to get that return." Hyatt said he rarely touches his stock portfolio, as tempting as it is with wildly gyrating markets and rising interest rates. He said the family office largely buys Vanguard ETF's, along with a handful of his favorite stocks, which include Google, Microsoft and Apple. With real estate, Hyatt has invested in a fund that buys commercial properties in secondary cities — a trade that's generated strong returns after the pandemic when many residents of big urban hubs moved to smaller cities but still wanted office space. The private equity and venture capital bucket of the portfolio is where Hyatt says he can "scratch his entrepreneurial itch" to find promising start-ups and help them grow. He mainly chooses funds where the founders also have substantial capital at risk and that are largely closed to medium-sized or small investors. The jockey, not the horse When it comes to investing directly in start-ups, Hyatt said he bets on the entrepreneur more than the idea, since every successful company makes big pivots in strategy. "I spend time investing in the jockey not the horse," he said. "And then I help figure it out." Hyatt said the key to a successful family office can be summed up in one word: no. "They don't say no enough," he said. "Just because I made the money doesn't mean I know how to invest it. I'm self aware enough to know that I'm wrong. When you say no to 100 things, there are going to be a couple that you say no to that are just incredible. And that's the point. But on average you really have to be disciplined."

Michael and Richard Hyatt have acquired a majority stake in Mississauga-based DataStealth, an enterprise cybersecurity firm that helps banks and hospitals protect their data.

For the brothers—both successful Canadian tech entrepreneurs-turned-investors who previously built, scaled, sold, and exited Toronto-based Dyadem and BlueCat in deals totalling more than $1 billion—the transaction marks a return to operations.

The Hyatts believe that they could have their “next big thing” with significant ownership of an efficient and fast-growing cybersecurity business at a time when cyber attacks are on the rise.

“We’re back, we’re doing something big, and this is super important to us,” Michael Hyatt told BetaKit in an interview. “We’ve now picked a horse and we’re all in on it.”

The Hyatt brothers’ majority stake investment closed earlier this month. Hyatt declined to disclose the price tag.

Speaking to the appeal of bringing on the Hyatts as investors, DataStealth co-founder and CEO Ed Leavens noted the pair’s experience building large, successful software companies, complementary skill sets, and willingness to “roll up their sleeves.”

“They took BlueCat to $100-million-plus in annual revenue, profitable—everything that we want to do, they just did this, and they did it twice,” Leavens told BetaKit in an interview. “We have a very solid foundation … We decided that we wanted to really grow, and [that] we needed some expertise, and we found our expertise.”

Founded in 2014, DataStealth aims to help large businesses protect their most sensitive data and documents. Built on its patented technology, the company sells a suite of products that tap into organizations’ networks to discover, classify, and protect data by tokenizing, encrypting, or masking it. DataStealth caters to a variety of industries, including telecommunications firms, financial institutions, insurance firms, and healthcare organizations.

According to Leavens, while other firms offer products that look like DataStealth’s offerings, what sets DataStealth apart from other players is its ease-of-use and speed of deployment. “The difference isn’t in what we do necessarily, it’s more about how we do it,” he said.

“It’s very simple—the technology just works,” added Hyatt. “You can install this product with no agent, no code, nothing. It just works.”

Hyatt was first introduced to DataStealth after one of the startup’s senior leaders asked him for advice. When Hyatt lent a hand and peeked under the hood, he said he was shocked at what he found: a profitable company with great technology, solid growth, strong gross margins, no debt, and limited outside capital, that was generating over $10 million in annual revenue.

“The amount of companies that are growing beautifully that have profit and no venture capital [funding] is incredible,” said Hyatt. “It’s very rare.”

Prior to the Hyatt brothers, DataStealth had just one external investor: a majority shareholder named Abe Schwartz. According to Leavens, he and DataStealth co-founder and CIO Marc Carrafiello used a ‘shotgun clause’ to buy out Schwartz for nearly $7 million, or $1.16 per share, and then sold a portion of Schwartz’s stake to the Hyatt brothers in a separate transaction.

Per an Ontario Superior Court of Justice ruling obtained by BetaKit, Schwartz initially took the position that this notice from Leavens and Carrafiello was improper and declined to respond, and pursued other legal action. However, an Ontario judge ruled in May that by not exercising his right to buy out Leavens and Carrafiello at the same price they offered for his stake, Schwartz accepted their offer, enforced the sale, and dismissed other issues brought up by Schwartz.

Speaking to DataStealth’s use of this shotgun clause, Leavens said, “I think that shotgun or buy-sell provisions in shareholder agreements are common, and we had an opportunity to take advantage of ours, so we did. That’s really all it was. And I think that we saw a different future.”

DataStealth has retained its management and roughly 45-person team as part of the deal. Per Leavens, the company’s leadership still holds a “significant piece of equity” in DataStealth.

“We decided that we wanted to really grow, and [that] we needed some expertise, and we found our expertise.”

– Ed Leavens, DataStealth

Hyatt has become executive chairman, and plans to focus his attention on DataStealth’s sales and go-to-market efforts, while Richard, who has also joined the board, is working with the startup’s engineering team.

“This is not a passive investment,” said Hyatt. “We’re working side by side with the executive team to help them grow and scale the business.”

Over the next few years, Hyatt said that their focus will be on scaling DataStealth’s business without taking on additional outside capital. He sees plenty of potential for DataStealth.

“Right now, we have so much runway,” said Hyatt. “Cybersecurity is so big. We think this outcome could be another BlueCat.”

--

BetaKit on November 1, 2023

and was authored by Josh Scott.

Michael Hyatt is a Canadian entrepreneur and investor recognized for his significant contributions to the technology sector. He co-founded BlueCat Networks, a company specializing in DNS security and management, which was acquired by Madison Dearborn Partners in 2017. Prior to BlueCat, he co-founded Dyadem, a software company that was acquired by IHS in 2011. These ventures have established him as a prominent figure in Canada's tech industry.

In addition to his entrepreneurial endeavors, Michael serves as a Senior Advisor to Northleaf Capital Partners, supporting their venture capital and growth equity investment program. He is also a Founding Partner and Fellow at the Rotman School of Management’s Creative Destruction Lab, a program designed to help early-stage science and technology companies build large, scalable, and impactful businesses. His involvement in these initiatives underscores his commitment to fostering innovation and supporting the growth of emerging companies.

Beyond his business activities, Michael is an active philanthropist, chairing the Hyatt Family Foundation, which focuses on women's health, critical hospital research, and support for underprivileged minorities. He also serves as a weekly business commentator on CBC and has been featured on the cover of Canadian Business Magazine. His diverse roles and contributions highlight his dedication to both business and community development.

Michael's investment philosophy centers on identifying and nurturing high-potential companies across various stages of growth. His strategic approach combines his extensive experience in building and scaling businesses with a keen eye for emerging opportunities, making him a valuable asset to the ventures he supports.

Through his ventures and investments, Michael Hyatt continues to play a pivotal role in shaping the landscape of Canada's technology sector, demonstrating a strong commitment to innovation, entrepreneurship, and social responsibility.

We are announcing our Venture Capital Fund 3 today. Coincidentally, it has been seven years this week since I first joined

Wittington Ventures

to build a venture investing business, and it's worth reflecting on how far the platform has come.

We started with one $100 million venture capital fund, a small team and a simple idea: combine disciplined start-up investing in the commerce and healthcare sectors with the long-term perspective and operating experience found across the Weston group of companies.

Seven years later, the Wittington Ventures platform looks very different.

Today, we invest across the three stages of the private-company journey: pre-seed / seed, venture capital, and growth. Our platform consists of a $100 million early-stage strategy, $400 million across three venture funds, and $320 million in growth capital. The team has grown to 15 people, we have invested in over 25 portfolio companies, and our sectors of investment have expanded beyond commerce and healthcare to now include consumer, food and climate verticals.

The numbers matter not because getting bigger was the objective, but because they show what the platform is now capable of doing:

Our Early-Stage strategy is focused entirely in Canadian deep-tech, helping bridge the critical funding gap between research and commercialization. We take a venture-studio approach to creating companies that solve big problems by commercializing Canadian research that we truly believe in. And our recently announced Weston Breakthrough Fellows program funds Canadian researcher-founders at their earliest stage of company formation. cc Zeeshan,

Vancouver startup Border0 is joining Toronto-based Tailscale — bringing together two companies building at different layers of the same problem: secure access.

Tailscale has become a go-to platform for identity-based connectivity — making it simple for devices and services to talk securely.

Border0, meanwhile, has been tackling what happens after that connection is made:
→ Who gets access
→ To what systems
→ For how long
→ And with what visibility

Put together, this starts to look a lot like a full-stack approach to modern infrastructure access.

As Tailscale CEO Avery Pennarun puts it, the conversation quickly shifted from “Can we partner?” to “What could we build together?”

For Border0 founder Andree Toonk, the vision has always been clear: make infrastructure access secure without making it painful.

The result: A tighter integration between connectivity and authorization — and a step toward a more complete, identity-first security platform.

Jan 26, 2022

Northleaf announces appointment of technology entrepreneur Michael Hyatt as a Senior Advisor to its venture capital and growth equity program

News

Private Equity

Northleaf

TORONTO, CANADA (January 26, 2022)

– Northleaf Capital Partners (“Northleaf”), a global private markets investment firm, is pleased to announce the appointment of Michael Hyatt as a Senior Advisor supporting Northleaf’s venture capital and growth equity investment program. Michael will work alongside the Northleaf private equity and venture capital team to source and evaluate investment opportunities. As a serial entrepreneur and active investor, Michael’s knowledge and expertise in the venture capital space complements Northleaf’s longstanding investment approach.

"We are excited to welcome Michael to Northleaf as a Senior Advisor,” said Ian Carew, Managing Director & Venture Partner at Northleaf. “We have invested successfully with Michael in the past and our venture capital and growth equity program will benefit from his deep knowledge and experience and accomplished track record as both an entrepreneur and investor.”

“I am thrilled to act as a Senior Advisor to Northleaf’s successful venture capital and growth equity program and look forward to working with Ian and the team,” said Michael Hyatt. “I’ve had the opportunity to see the Northleaf strategy at work over the years and I’m excited to collaborate with the team on future investments for the program.”

Michael Hyatt is recognized as one of Canada’s leading tech entrepreneurs and an active investor in the technology community. He is the co-founder of BlueCat (in which Northleaf was an early investor and which was acquired by a private equity firm in 2017) and previously co-founded Dyadem (a software company that was sold to IHS in 2011). He currently serves as a Director of BlueCat. Michael is a regular business commentator on the CBC and the host of “Unplanned Business,” a podcast to help small businesses. He is a Founding Partner at the Rotman School of Management’s prestigious Creative Destruction Lab (CDL) and chairs the Hyatt Family Foundation focused on women’s health, critical hospital research and sponsorship of underprivileged minorities.

Northleaf is one of Canada’s most active venture capital investors. Northleaf manages more than US$800 million in venture capital and growth equity commitments on behalf of investors and has played a leadership role in the development of many successful venture capital / growth equity funds. Northleaf has been making direct investments in later-stage and high growth companies since 2008, leveraging its well-established relationships with leading fund managers, institutional investors and entrepreneurs.

About Northleaf Capital Partners

Northleaf Capital Partners is a global private markets investment firm with more than US$19 billion in private equity and venture capital, private credit and infrastructure commitments under management on behalf of public, corporate and multi-employer pension plans, endowments, foundations, financial institutions and family offices. Northleaf’s team of more than 160 professionals, located in Toronto, Chicago, London, Melbourne, Menlo Park, Montreal and New York, is focused exclusively on sourcing, evaluating and managing private markets investments globally. Its portfolio includes over 400 active investments in 40 countries, with a focus on mid-market companies and assets. For more information on Northleaf, please visit

www.northleafcapital.com

BMO Unveils New Podcast for Canadian Businesses
Accessibility Statement
Skip Navigation
BMO reaffirms commitment as the bank for business with content focused on business resiliency and growth to help clients make real financial progress
Well-known entrepreneur and investor Michael Hyatt headlines as the host of the podcast
TORONTO, June 25, 2020 /CNW/ - BMO has today introduced a new podcast dedicated to Canadian businesses. The podcast – Business Unplanned – will provide business owners with expert opinions and advice on business resiliency and adaptability during this uncertain time. This announcement builds off of the bank's recently introduced online resource hub and will provide Canadian businesses with an additional resource to help their long-term growth.
"We are helping thousands of businesses across geographies and sectors every week and are constantly looking for opportunities to do more," said Erminia (Ernie) Johannson, Group Head, North American Personal and Business Banking, BMO Financial Group. "In conversations with our clients, we heard how important and beneficial it is for them to have a community where they can learn from each other. We have now created an additional resource where businesses can come together and learn from entrepreneurs and business owners and apply best practices to their own businesses."
Business Unplanned will feature six episodes and be available on bmo.com/BusinessUnplanned as well as on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and Google Podcasts. Episodes will be released periodically throughout the summer. Entrepreneur, investor, and co-founder of BlueCat, Michael Hyatt, has joined as the host of Business Unplanned. He will lead listeners on a journey as they dive into stories from leading entrepreneurs and small business owners.
"More than ever before, leaders need to come together to help both small businesses and the wider business community overcome the challenges of this pandemic," said Mr. Hyatt. "Joining BMO as the host of Business Unplanned is a way to do that and provides an outlet where business owners can relate to what we are sharing and take away actionable advice for their business."
The podcast will include guests from a range of sectors and business size and will cover:
Episode 1: The Business Recovery
Episode 2: Making Business Adjustments: How to Plan Post-Pandemic
Episode 3: Getting a Business Loan During Covid-19
Episode 4: Managing Cash Flow Post-Covid-19
Episode 5: How to Stay Motivated in Business
Episode 6: Understanding Customers' Needs
To access BMO's Business Resource Hub, visit: https://www.bmo.com/main/business/small-business-resource-hub/.
To stay connected with BMO or to access the bank's new online support tool, visit: bmo.com/covid19.
About BMO Financial Group
Serving customers for 200 years and counting, BMO is a highly diversified financial services provider - the 8th largest bank, by assets, in North America. With total assets of $987 billion as of April 30, 2020, and a team of diverse and highly engaged employees, BMO provides a broad range of personal and commercial banking, wealth management and investment banking products and services to more than 12 million customers and conducts business through three operating groups: Personal and Commercial Banking, BMO Wealth Management and BMO Capital Markets.
Internet: www.bmo.com Twitter: @BMOmedia

Michael & Vanessa Hyatt

Area of Expertise
Vanessa is a Senior Counsel at RBC. Prior to joining RBC, Vanessa was a litigation counsel at the Department of Justice Canada, specializing in a broad range of complex legal and policy matters involving social benefits programs and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Vanessa regularly represented the Attorney General of Canada before the Federal Court and the Federal Court of Appeal.
Vanessa is on the Board of Directors of International Planned Parenthood Federation / Western Hemisphere Region and of IPPF Canada. She was a guest speaker on women empowerment at the International Women’s Empowerment and Leadership Conference and at the Women’s Festival Toronto Gala. She has volunteered for the Elizabeth Fry Society of Ottawa, which supports and advocates for young and adult women who are criminalized or may become criminalized. She earned both a JD and a License of Civil Law from the University of Ottawa. Vanessa speaks English, French and Spanish fluently.
Michael Hyatt is the co-founder of BlueCat, which was sold to Madison Dearborn Partners, of Chicago, IL. He serves as a director of BlueCat, ranks as one of Canada’s top entrepreneurs, and is known as a technology visionary. Michael is also a weekly business commentator on CBC and was a celebrated “Dragon” on CBC’s online Dragons’ Den. He is the Host of BMO’s Unplanned Business podcast to help small businesses and an investor on the hit Spotify podcast “The Pitch”. Michael is a Founding Partner and Fellow at the Rotman School of Management’s prestigious Creative Destruction Lab and sits on the CEO Board of Advisors of Georgian Partners, one of Canada’s leading venture capital firms. He was also recently named Entrepreneur in Residence (EIR) at Blakes, one of the most successful law firms in the country.

It is with pleasure and gratitude that I welcome you to 
the 8th Canadian Alternative Investment Forum.
From our long standing position as a neutral industry 
player, Introduction Capital continues to gain more 
and more access to niche alternative investment ideas 
that we thoughtfully integrate into CAIF’s agenda.  
We have noticed a paradigm shift, a positive uptick 
in momentum and enthusiasm amongst clients and 
colleagues this past year. This has been quite exciting 
and is reflected through significant interest in our 
conference and in the other lines of our business.
A colleague asked recently, how CAIF began and I 
smiled reminiscing how the state of the economy had 
served as a catalyst to create something new, and 
something needed!
Introduction Capital had produced three conferences 
called, “Canadian Hedge Fund Managers Speak with 
Investors Forum” in ‘06, ‘07 and lastly in ‘08. Almost 
every Canadian hedge fund manager from that era 
participated and the investors came to hear from them.  
I don’t need to remind anyone in this room that all hell 
broke loose in the financial sector shortly thereafter, and 
so we correctly put the conference on hold.
In 2010, having weathered the financial storm, we 
decided to create a conference reflecting our new 
economy, that would include the whole range of 
alternative investments, well beyond just hedge funds.  
I had a sense that if we created the environment for 
cross-pollination, everyone would collectively benefit.  
Grounded in this measured intention, we have 
continued for eight years to produce a unique forum 
filled with bright ideas, meaningful connections,  
and a fertile environment for innovative  
opportunities to emerge.
With the support of a great team, our speakers and 
sponsors, CAIF has continually remained fresh, 
original and special. 
In keeping with our mission, we hope that you 
will experience this year’s conference as relevant, 
educational and uplifting.
We are very proud of our speaker line-up this year 
and grateful to all of our generous sponsors for their 
ongoing support. Thank you for joining us today! 
Wishing you abundance in every area of your life, 
today and always.
