Most AI agents forget everything the moment you close the chat window. Hermes Agent was built to fix exactly that.
And honestly, once you understand how it works, it is hard to go back to thinking about agents the old way.
Most agent frameworks follow the same basic loop. You give it a task, it executes, it returns a result, and the session ends. Next time you open it, it has no idea who you are, what you prefer, or how it solved something similar last week. You start from zero every single time.
Hermes Agent, built by Nous Research, is designed around a completely different idea.
So how does it actually work?
Traditional agent:
User input ➡️ Plan ➡️ Execute ➡️ Return result ➡️ Session ends ➡️ Memory wiped
Hermes agent:
User input ➡️ Load memory + skills ➡️ Plan + retrieve ➡️ Execute ➡️ Evaluate + extract ➡️ Save skills + session log + user model ➡️ Feeds back into next session
After completing a complex task, the agent does not just return the result and move on. It evaluates what it did, extracts the reasoning pattern, and saves it as a reusable skill. Next time a similar task comes up, it loads that skill and applies it. And if a better approach comes along, the skill gets updated automatically.
The memory system is just as thoughtful. It maintains two persistent files: one for environment facts, conventions, and lessons learned, and one for your preferences and communication style. Both get injected into the system prompt at the start of every session. It also has full-text search over all past conversations stored in SQLite, so it can pull up how it handled something three weeks ago.
Here is what makes this genuinely interesting.
It is not tied to a single LLM provider or a single platform. You can run it on a $5 VPS, plug in OpenAI, Anthropic, or a local model via Ollama, and chat with it over Telegram, Slack, Discord, or your terminal. The conversation continues across all of them.
The agent you are using in month three is measurably more capable than the one you started with, because it has been learning from your actual workflows the entire time.
Persistent memory is not a nice-to-have feature in an agent, it is the whole point.

Sora is dead.
With all the talk of people now being able to write a million lines of code in a week, we are seeing OpenAI finally start to put a little focus into their business and drop things that are doing more damage than good.
Email is now, just about, as useless as most of the internet.
Bots writing to each other and humans starting to stay outside the loop.
Many people tell me they are now only checking email a couple of times a month.
Social platforms are less and less interesting - never mind useful.
We forget too quickly that just because we *can* do something, doesn't mean we _should_ do it.
People aren't just going to create their own tools - generally speaking. We purchase tools like Office or Workspace not only because they do what we need them to, but because we don't want to maintain those codebases.
I know, I know ... Jensen Huang's jacket says that we won't need to maintain code - use agents to build it *and* to maintain it.
Good luck with that.
People *will* use AI to create tools that don't have a large market - tools that specifically serve them. I just did it so I could have a polywav splitter and batch convert polwavs to individual wav files.
It's awesome. I am not anti-AI, agents, or whatever other terms the marketers come up with.
But, people who are selling tokens are gonna sell tokens. And tokens can't stay subsidized forever.
We saw the same playbook with SaaS, with Cloud, with IaS, and with just about everything else created and sold over the last hundred years.
What's this post about? Nothing really. It's just me reacting in public to the things I keep seeing, which I think are mostly nonsense.
But, the playbook is the same, always - work through the nonsense to get to the upside.
Will be the same this time around, too.

The Most Underrated Canadian Founder You’ve Probably Never Heard Of
If Michael Hyatt were American, he’d have 500,000 LinkedIn followers, a book deal, and a Netflix documentary called “How to Print Money Legally.”
But he’s Canadian…
So nobody talks about him.
Let’s fix that.
Meet Michael Hyatt: the quiet Canadian who sold not one, but TWO huge companies before he turned 30.
Everyone knows Shopify.
Everyone knows Lululemon.
But almost nobody knows the guy who built one of Canada’s most valuable cybersecurity firms and sold it for $400M+, and then just kept going.
This is why I love studying founders like Hyatt:
They aren’t loud.
They aren’t flashy.
They just win.
The Story
At 17, he’s playing with servers while the rest of us were trying to get a date to grad.
At 25, he starts his first tech company, Dyadem.
At 29, he sells it.
Then he does the most un-Canadian thing ever:
He starts another one.
That company?
BlueCat.
The invisible plumbing behind the internet that no one thinks about until it breaks.
Think cybersecurity meets infrastructure meets “oh God don’t let this fail.”
Everyone said building it in Canada was impossible.
Hyatt built it anyway.
Scaled it.
Then sold it for hundreds of millions.
Instead of buying a yacht and disappearing to Anguilla, he becomes an angel investor, backs dozens of companies, becomes a CBC Dragon, gives straight-talk business advice, and mentors founders across the country.
No ego.
No influencer vibes.
Just results.
Why I’m Obsessed With His Playbook
Here’s the thing about Hyatt:
He didn’t build a social app.
He didn’t build a marketplace.
He built boring infrastructure that powers the internet.
And boring infrastructure is where the money is.
His lessons hit hard:
Solve real problems, “not founder feelings.”
Ignore hype, focus on customers who pay.
Build discipline, not dopamine.
Be relentless, even when nobody sees you.
Think decades, not quarters.
Canada desperately needs more founders like him, quiet killers who build important things instead of shiny things.
The Takeaway
Canada has a lot of amazing founders building amazing things.
They’re the ones who don’t go viral.
They don’t chase clout.
They build internet plumbing, cybersecurity rails, utilities, enterprise tools, the stuff billion-dollar companies rely on.
Hyatt is the blueprint:
Start small
Build something real
Sell it
Do it again
Help others
Simple.
Not easy.
If you’re building something in Canada, study this man.
He’s one of our country’s best founders.
We just haven’t built him a statue yet.

Keys to Greatness: Michael Hyatt (DataStealth)
G — Genesis
Michael Hyatt’s foundation was built in the evolving world of cybersecurity, where data became the new currency—and the new vulnerability. He identified a critical gap: organizations were collecting massive amounts of sensitive data but lacked true control over how it was accessed, monitored, and protected. This insight sparked the creation of DataStealth.
O — Organization
Hyatt structured DataStealth around precision and adaptability. Instead of one-size-fits-all security, the company delivers tailored data protection strategies—monitoring, masking, and controlling access at the data level.
A — Action Plan
Execution is where Hyatt stands out. He translated complex cybersecurity challenges into actionable solutions—real-time monitoring, data activity tracking, and risk mitigation tools.
L — Leverage
Hyatt leveraged emerging trends in data privacy regulations and enterprise risk management to position DataStealth as a necessary solution, not a luxury. By aligning with compliance demands (HIPAA, GDPR, etc.), he turned regulatory pressure into business opportunity.
S — Synergy
The synergy in Hyatt’s model comes from integrating security with business operations. DataStealth doesn’t just protect data—it enhances decision-making by providing clarity on how data is used. This alignment between security, compliance, and operational intelligence creates a powerful, unified value proposition.
E — Education/Experience
Hyatt’s deep experience in cybersecurity and enterprise data systems gives him technical authority and strategic insight. He understands both the architecture of systems and the risks within them.
F — Focus
His focus is sharp: protect the data itself. While many chase network security, Hyatt zeroes in on the asset—data—making his approach both differentiated and future-proof.
F — Formidable
Operating in cybersecurity requires constant evolution. Hyatt built a formidable company capable of adapting to new threats, regulations, and technologies—staying ahead in a high-stakes industry.
O — Organization (Execution Discipline)
DataStealth’s solutions reflect disciplined execution—structured, reliable, and scalable. This consistency builds trust with enterprise clients where failure is not an option.
R — Risk
Entering a crowded cybersecurity space required strategic risk. Hyatt differentiated by narrowing focus to data-centric security—a bold move that carved out a distinct niche.
T — Teamwork
Cybersecurity is a team sport. Hyatt built a team of experts capable of addressing complex enterprise challenges, ensuring that innovation and protection evolve together.
Bottom Line
Michael Hyatt’s greatness lies in seeing what others overlooked—the data itself—and building systems to control, monitor, and protect it at the highest level. Through clarity of focus and disciplined execution, he transformed cybersecurity from reactive defense into proactive data intelligence.

There is a pattern I have watched repeat itself across more than 15 years working in information security, data protection, and enterprise risk. Every few years, a new term rises to the top of every conference agenda, every board deck, every vendor pitch. Right now, that term is AI governance. Before that, it was Zero Trust. Before that, compliance frameworks. Before that, GDPR.
Each wave arrives with a sense of urgency — as if the industry has discovered something entirely new. Each wave attracts enormous attention, investment, and debate. And each time, the same foundational question goes quietly unanswered: have we actually built the thing that makes all of this work?
Because here is what I have observed, consistently and across many organisations: the buzzword changes. The underlying principle does not.
It Started With a Simple Idea — Protect the Environment
Cast your mind back to the early days of information security. The model was straightforward. Organisations operated within sealed network perimeters. If you were inside the boundary, you were trusted. If you were outside, you were not. Security meant building a strong enough wall.
That worked for a while. Then digitalisation arrived, and with it, the imperative to connect. Being able to operate across systems, grant access to clients and third parties, and develop as a business online stopped being optional. The perimeter dissolved. And the model had to change.
From my own experience, that shift accelerated significantly around 2010. The focus moved from protecting networks to protecting data — wherever it lived, wherever it travelled, whoever touched it.
The Standard That Changed the Conversation
In this context, the information security industry began to formalise its thinking. The roots go back to 1995, when the British Standards Institution published BS 7799, an early code of best practices for information security management. The concept of the Information Security Management System (ISMS) was introduced in BS 7799-2 in 1998, and in 2005, it became the first internationally recognised standard: ISO/IEC 27001:2005. [1]
The most recent version, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, updated the standard further to address cloud computing, remote work, and modern threat landscapes. [3]
ISO 27001 introduced more than just a checklist. It was a system — built on a deceptively simple principle: that protecting data is not an IT function. It is a business function. And for it to work, it must be embedded across the entire organisation, aligned with business goals and objectives, and brought to every level of the enterprise.
That was the foundation. That was the holistic approach. Strategy first. Alignment second. Controls third — not the other way around.
Then the Cycles Began
What followed was a series of waves, each one picking up one thread from that foundational model and pulling it to the front.....

Step 2: Establish Current Maturity
With key risks and assets identified, the next step is to assess the design and operating effectiveness of existing controls. This benchmarking should be aligned to industry standards such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, ISO/IEC 27001, or the CIS Controls — both to ensure completeness and to present credible findings to the board.
A gap analysis across key domains — governance, risk assessment, supply
chain, and technical controls — puts a stake in the ground and directs limited resources toward areas of highest risk. It also gives the cyber leader a clear basis for setting a forward-looking vision and keeping the board informed on how investments are improving the organization’s risk profile.
Step 3: Define a High-Value Strategy
With a clear picture of current strengths and gaps, the cyber leader must develop a multi-year security strategy aligned to organizational objectives. This means building a three-year roadmap with defined priorities, actions, outcomes, and accountabilities — one that addresses the most critical risks first, delivers early wins, and meets regulatory and customer requirements.
The primary goal should be to build security capabilities the organization can sustain, rather than acquiring additional tools for their own sake. Implementing robust threat detection and response — with defined processes, skilled people, and appropriate technology — often reduces risk more effectively than investing in the latest tools. Focusing on capabilities over features is the surest way to ensure security investments deliver meaningful, long-term improvement.
Step 4: Build the Business Case and Secure Funding
With a clear plan in hand, the cyber leader must develop a compelling business case that articulates the problem or opportunity, the proposed solution, expected benefits, cost, and resource requirements, risk analysis, and a return on investment. Each initiative should be linked to measurable outcomes — reduced risk, improved compliance, or increased operational efficiency.
To gain approval, funding, and executive support, present a phased plan that balances long-term ambition with near-term delivery. Highlighting quick wins within the first 90 days — such as closing critical control gaps or strengthening oversight of high-risk assets — builds momentum and earns the confidence of key stakeholders.

🌫️ Organizations often believe they are resilient when systems remain available, processes continue, and dashboards stay green. Yet an enterprise can appear stable while quietly weakening at its seams. A public platform may remain online even as sensitive data is exposed. A trusted outsourcing workflow may continue operating while HR records slip into unsafe hands. A finance process may complete as designed while funds are diverted to an attacker. An AI coding tool may increase productivity while also expanding the reach of privileged software and fueling malware campaigns driven by curiosity and urgency. What looks like resilience can be a carefully maintained illusion of control.
🧩 The common lesson across these cases is that cyber risk rarely collapses an enterprise in one dramatic moment. More often, it accumulates in areas leaders are most likely to treat as secondary: workforce readiness, cloud-facing services, third-party transfer points, payment verification routines, release engineering, telemetry boundaries, and developer behavior during moments of intense attention. NIST’s emphasis on aligning cyber risk, enterprise priorities, and workforce capability fits this reality closely, because gaps in skills, accountability, and governance do not remain administrative for long. They become operational exposure. The deeper weakness is not simply inadequate security tooling. It is the separation of business continuity from confidentiality, compliance from maturity, outsourcing from ownership, and AI productivity from software governance.
🛡️ One of the most dangerous signals in modern cybersecurity is a process that is still functioning. Operations may continue even as loss is spreading through the workflows the business trusts most. Resilience, therefore, cannot be defined by uptime alone. It must also include the ability to preserve trust, data integrity, decision quality, and institutional credibility under pressure. In practice, that requires tighter governance over third-party handoffs, stronger validation for financially sensitive changes, clearer control over AI agent permissions, disciplined software release pipelines, restrained telemetry practices, and executive ownership of workforce capability as a risk issue rather than merely a staffing concern. The organizations most likely to succeed in this environment will not be those that simply keep operating. They will be the ones that can prove they are operating safely, deliberately, and with trust still intact.
💬 Where in your environment does resilience look strongest on the surface, yet depend most on fragile trust underneath? Have you seen continuity metrics create a false sense of security while confidentiality, governance, or accountability were quietly weakening?

🔹 Network security benefits from operational dashboards

The blog /Link post by Adaptive Information Systems explores a critical business scenario — what happens when an organization loses all its data, including files, customer records, invoices, and operational data. It highlights that the consequences can be devastating, ranging from downtime and lost revenue to compliance violations and even permanent business closure. The article covers the common causes of data loss — cyberattacks, hardware failures, and accidental deletions — and focuses on prevention strategies.
💥 Impact of Business Data Loss
Downtime alone can cost small businesses thousands of dollars per hour, and recovering lost data — if even possible — is expensive and time-consuming.
Around 43% of all cyberattacks target smaller companies because they are easier to break into, and an estimated 60% of these small businesses shut down within six months of a major attack. Additionally, 40% of businesses hit by ransomware lost important data, and 51% of those affected paid the criminals.
🔑 Key Prevention Strategies
1. Backup & Disaster Recovery (BDR) A BDR plan works in the background, making copies of important business data and storing them in a separate, secure location. If main systems are compromised, it enables rapid restoration and minimizes downtime.
2. Recovery Objectives Two critical metrics guide any recovery plan — Recovery Time Objective (RTO), which defines how fast systems must be restored, and Recovery Point Objective (RPO), which defines how much recent data loss is acceptable. These two goals form the foundation of a business continuity strategy.
3. Ransomware Defense When ransomware locks your files, having a clean backup is often the only way to get back to business without paying the criminals.
4. Human Firewall — Employee Training Cybercriminals often bypass tough firewalls by sending convincing emails to employees. Building a human firewall through security awareness training makes employees the first line of defense rather than the weakest link.
5. Proactive Monitoring Infrastructure monitoring acts as a 24/7 health checkup for all business technology — catching small issues before they escalate into major failures that can shut operations down entirely.
6. Access Controls & MFA The biggest threat to personal data is unauthorized access. Storing sensitive information on a robust cloud platform with correct permission settings, multi-factor authentication (MFA), and restricted user access is essential to preventing breaches.

1.Perform a cybersecurity risk assessment
Enterprises must ensure regular evaluation of the impact of any crisis on their digital and operational systems. At the outset, it is important to take inventory of all digital assets and evaluate if all security controls, such as access controls and encryption, are in place. Simulate real-world attacks and conduct penetration testing to assess the defenses. This exercise helps in identifying, analyzing, and prioritizing critical risks caused by common security threats and the presence of vulnerabilities such as weak passwords or outdated software.
2.Implement Zero Trust Architecture
Traditional perimeter-based security models fail in today’s digital age,where hybrid and remote work cultures and cloud adoption are prevalent. Zero-trust architecture addresses this challenge by following the principle of ‘never trust, always verify’. This model performs continuous verification, enforces least privilege access, and constantly monitors all user activities.
3.Build cyber resilient supply chain and operations
Emergencies often disrupt global supply chains and expose vulnerabilities within partner ecosystems. Several organizations share sensitive data with suppliers, which is stored with them. If the vendors do not follow strong cybersecurity practices, in the event of a security breach, attackers gain access to data that is now with the suppliers.
When such incidents are not reported, organizations are not even aware of the security breaches
4.Implement advanced threat detection and security operations frameworks
With advanced technologies such as AI and machine learning, organizations are able to automate detection while identifying threats at scale. AI-driven Agentic Security Operations Centers (SOCs) can analyze huge volumes of data to detect anomalies and low-noise intrusions in real-time. Behavioral biometrics analyzes user behavior and detects patterns to identify potential threats
5.Business continuity and disaster recovery planning
Cyber incidents, data breaches, and AI-driven deep fakes and frauds are pervasive and evolving, impacting organizations and individuals. Organizations have to ensure operational resilience even during cybersecurity incidents or any crisis by implementing comprehensive business continuity and disaster recovery strategies. High-risk digital assets and services are to be identified, and mission-critical data documented. Having a response plan for incidents and ensuring they align with the organization’s business continuity strategy is key. Rapid system recovery mechanisms should be in place with organizations following the 3-2-1 backup rule. Backup recovery must be evaluated regularly. The aim is to recover the data and restore the business function with minimum disruption.

5 Principles for Achieving Sustainable Work-Life Balance with Michael & Megan Hyatt
November 4, 2024
Michael Hyatt is the Founder and Chairman of Full Focus. He has scaled multiple companies over the years, including a $250M publishing company with 700+ employees and his own goal-achievement company. Michael is also the author of several New York Times, Wall Street Journal, and USA Today bestselling books. He has been married for over 45 years to his wife Gail, has five daughters, and ten grandchildren.
Megan Hyatt Miller is the President and Chief Executive Officer of Full Focus, co-host of the popular Double Win podcast, and Wall Street Journal bestselling author of Mind Your Mindset and Win at Work & Succeed at Life. All of this while finishing every day by 3 pm, so she and her husband, Joel, can be fully present with their five kids when they get home from school.
This content contains affiliate links. If you use these links to purchase something, we may earn a commission. Thanks.
Is achieving a work-life balance a realistic goal in today’s modern age?
It can often feel like there is no winning when it comes to balancing all areas of your life. Working long hours usually results in less sleep. You have more time for meetings, but less time for friends and family. But there’s good news. It’s possible to give every area of your life the attention it needs so you can thrive.
Our guests today are more than familiar with this dilemma and they’ve found a way around it. Most businesses don't fail at AI because the technology is too complex. They fail because they skip the strategy.
Before you buy another tool or run another ChatGPT experiment, it helps to have a clear framework. Here's a simple 4-step AI strategy blueprint that actually works for small and mid-sized businesses.
🔍 Step 1: Audit your operations. Identify the repetitive, time-consuming tasks that drain your team every week. These are your highest-value automation targets.
Step 2: Set clear goals. AI works best when it's solving a specific problem, not just "doing AI things." Tie every initiative to a measurable outcome, whether that's reducing response time, cutting costs, or improving lead quality.
Step 3: Start with one workflow. Pick the single highest-impact process and build there first. A focused pilot gives you proof of ROI before you scale, and keeps your team from getting overwhelmed.
⚙️ Step 4: Measure, learn, expand. Track what changes after implementation. Use those insights to refine your approach and roll out automation across more areas of the business.
This is exactly how businesses go from curious about AI to genuinely competitive with it. No hype, no expensive overhauls. Just a clear, repeatable process that builds real momentum over time.

Customers never see the puzzle, only the finished answer
Artificial intelligence assembles your business the way someone assembles a jigsaw puzzle. It gathers pieces from your website, directories, review sites, news articles, social profiles, and partner pages, then fits them together into one description.
Some pieces fit perfectly. Some overlap. Some belong to an older version of your business. A few may not belong to your business at all.
Your customer never sees any of that.
They ask ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude a question and receive one confident answer. They have no way to know whether that answer came from a puzzle that was assembled correctly or one that left out the wrong pieces.
That is the part most business owners never think about. You are not just being described. You are being assembled, piece by piece, from sources you may not even remember publishing.
Two businesses with nearly identical websites can receive completely different AI descriptions if one has years of consistent sources and the other has scattered, conflicting ones. The website looks the same to a person reading it. It does not look the same to AI trying to build a picture from every source it can find.
The only way to know what picture AI actually assembled is to see it laid out plainly instead of guessing from the finished answer.
The Frank Masotti AI Business Understanding Report shows you exactly how ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude currently describe your business, what pieces they used, and where the picture comes apart. Frank personally puts the puzzle back together so you can see it, not just the answer it produced.

Productivity and margin are related but distinct outcomes. Productivity means doing more. Margin means having space—financial, temporal, and personal—to make strategic choices rather than reactive ones.
Most AI education focuses on productivity: work faster, produce more, optimize harder. This framing often leads to the same overwork patterns, just accelerated.
The more valuable frame is margin creation. AI that recovers 10+ hours weekly doesn’t just increase output. It creates space for strategic thinking, relationship investment, personal renewal, and the kind of unhurried decision-making that drives long-term business health.
This is what I call the Double Win: better business results achieved with more personal freedom. Not one at the expense of the other.
The AI Business Lab® Mastermind is built around this thesis. We measure success not just in efficiency gains and cost savings, but in the quality of life our members are building alongside their business results.
Three annual intensives. Monthly sessions. Peer accountability. All oriented toward building AI-powered businesses that create margin, not just productivity.
A few spots remain.

The buzzword carousel is spinning faster than ever—and your customers are dizzy.
According to Forbes' latest research on thought leadership trends, "Humanity Beats Hype" is the #1 trend for 2026. And for SMBs, this couldn't be more timely.
Here's what's happening: While everyone's racing to slap "AI-powered" on everything, buyers are craving something different—authentic voices, real problems solved, and leaders who sound like humans, not press releases.
For small and medium businesses, this is actually your competitive advantage.
Consider a scenario where two companies offer similar solutions. Company A floods LinkedIn with "revolutionary AI" claims and generic automation talk. Company B shares honest insights about what's actually working, admits where they're still figuring things out, and focuses on customer outcomes over tech specs.
Which one builds trust faster?
The research shows a clear shift: quality beats quantity, depth beats breadth, and authenticity beats artificial hype. Your customers don't need another AI sermon—they need practical guidance from leaders who understand their real challenges.
Three ways SMBs can leverage this trend:
→ Share what you're genuinely learning, not what sounds impressive
→ Lead with customer problems, not your technology features
→ Build your voice around expertise and honesty, not jargon
The irony? In an age of artificial intelligence, the most valuable currency is authentic leadership.
What's one piece of "industry hype" you're deliberately avoiding in your business communications?
#ThoughtLeadership #AuthenticLeadership #SMBStrategy #B2BTrust #LeadershipTrends

𝐍𝐨𝐰 𝐢𝐭’𝐬 𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧 𝐢𝐭.
For years, professional services ran on a simple equation:
More people → More revenue.
But AI has changed the economics. The real question is no longer:
“𝘏𝘰𝘸 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘺 𝘍𝘛𝘌𝘴 𝘥𝘰 𝘸𝘦 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦?”
𝘐𝘵 𝘪𝘴:
“𝘏𝘰𝘸 𝘦𝘧𝘧𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘭𝘺 𝘥𝘰 𝘸𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘵 𝘤𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘰 𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘱𝘶𝘵?”
In my own experience, the biggest challenge is not cost increase or volume fluctuation—
It’s that our metrics were never designed for this new reality. So we started reframing the lens:
𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 → 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐨𝐢𝐬𝐞
𝐔𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 & 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐲 → 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭
𝐃𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐄𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐲 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐱 (𝐃𝐄𝐈) → 𝐛𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐢𝐭 𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐨𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫
𝐀𝐈 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 → 𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐮𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠
What this really does is simple:
It shifts the conversation from “𝘞𝘩𝘺 𝘪𝘴 𝘤𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘪𝘯𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘨?”
to “𝘈𝘳𝘦 𝘸𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘦𝘧𝘧𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘵?”
And that’s a fundamentally different leadership discussion.
The firms that win won’t be the ones with the largest teams. They’ll be the ones that engineer efficiency, not just manage capacity.
"𝑰𝒇 𝒚𝒐𝒖𝒓 𝒎𝒆𝒕𝒓𝒊𝒄𝒔 𝒔𝒕𝒊𝒍𝒍 𝒓𝒆𝒘𝒂𝒓𝒅 𝒆𝒇𝒇𝒐𝒓𝒕 𝒐𝒗𝒆𝒓 𝒆𝒇𝒇𝒊𝒄𝒊𝒆𝒏𝒄𝒚, 𝒚𝒐𝒖’𝒓𝒆 𝒂𝒍𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒅𝒚 𝒃𝒆𝒉𝒊𝒏𝒅"

Why the "Perfect" Strategy Fails Without the "Perfect" Synergy 🏗️✨
.
In the 2026 corporate landscape, we often obsess over Technology—specifically AI-driven workflows—thinking it's the silver bullet for growth.
But as this model illustrates, Technology is only one-third of the equation. To hit your Organizational Goals, three pillars must remain in perfect alignment within the ever-shifting External Environment:
.
STRUCTURE (The Skeleton): Clear hierarchy and rules aren’t about "control"; they are about providing a roadmap for decision-making.
.
PEOPLE (The Soul): Culture eats strategy for breakfast. If your team’s interactions and values don't align with the structure, the engine stalls.
.
TECHNOLOGY (The Catalyst): In 2026, AI isn't just a tool; it's a teammate. It must be integrated into the workflow, not just "added on."
.
The Reality Check: You can have the best AI in the world, but if your structure is rigid and your people are disengaged, you won't hit the target.
.

I have an intentional approach to how I talk about people, and I invite you to join me:
Organizations tend to:
-measure output.
-track performance.
-optimize for efficiency.
And now, with AI accelerating everything, it’s easy to believe that what people produce is all that really matters.
But here’s what I keep coming back to:
People are not their output.
They are their stories.
Their perspectives.
Their values.
Their lived experiences.
Their potential — much of which never shows up in a dashboard.
In every organization I’ve been part of, the real breakthroughs didn’t come from better metrics alone. They came from connection. From trust. From someone taking the time to truly see another human being.
AI will absolutely transform how we work. It should.
But it cannot replace what makes work meaningful — or what makes organizations thrive.
It cannot replicate:
• Genuine curiosity about another person
• The nuance of cultural understanding
• The trust built in a moment of vulnerability
• The energy of people who feel seen and valued
That’s not a limitation of technology. It’s a reminder of what matters most.
If our people strategies only evolve around efficiency, we risk losing the very thing that drives sustainable performance: human connection.
But if we design with people — not just productivity — at the center…
We don’t just build better organizations.
We build stronger, more human ones.
And that’s the kind of future I believe in.

Two organizations start the same week.
Same industry. Same size.
Same AI tools deployed. Same budget invested.
Six months later, one of them is operating with a measurably different intelligence advantage.
The other is still measuring adoption rates.
Here is what happened in between.
Organization A deployed the tools. Measured logins. Reported to the board that AI adoption was on track.
The model got smarter.
For everyone.
The competitive intelligence was exactly as generic on Month 6 as it was on Day 1.
Organization B deployed enablement sprints using UniversalContext Intelligence Platform and human enablement.
They connected their project history.
Their client communications. Their decision records.
They enables their teams to re-invent their workflows.
Share their institutional knowledge.
Every meeting, every document, every lesson from every engagement.
The model got smarter.
For them specifically.
By Month 3, Organization B's AI knew what their best people know.
By Month 6, it was producing insights their best people had never had time to surface.
The underlying models are identical. The competitive advantage is not.
This is the organizational intelligence argument.
Not which AI you run.
But enabling your AI to get smarter specifically about your organization.
The six-month divergence is real. And it compounds in one direction.
The organizations starting that investment now will be six months ahead of anyone starting next quarter.
That gap only grows.

Over lunch last week, an old friend told me the formula had changed.
He has spent more than a decade in outsourcing. Helping companies move work offshore in the name of efficiency and cost reduction. The maths used to be simple, he said.
Revenue = "Number of people × billing rate."
That equation shaped a generation of global work. Optimising labour. Distributing talent across continents. Squeezing inefficiency out of systems that ran on human input.
"Today," he continued, "it's outcome × AI leverage."
That shift says everything.
We are no longer just rethinking where work gets done. We are rethinking how it gets done. And increasingly, who or what does it.
The unit of value has changed. Human effort alone no longer carries the price. It is now human judgement combined with machine capability. The two together. Or in some cases, the machine on its own.
What happens to the role of people when outcomes can scale without scaling the humans behind them?
This question cuts into how we define contribution, purpose, and the dignity of work itself.
In Leading in the Age of AI, one of the threads I keep returning to is this. The hardest questions of this decade will not be technical. They will be moral. The Stoics understood that what you do with power matters far more than what power you hold. We are about to find out whether modern leadership has the same nerve.
That conversation over lunch is exactly why I wrote the book.

In professional services, onboarding new talent without compromising client experience is one of the most persistent operational challenges. Founders often become the bottleneck—personally training every hire because the stakes are too high to delegate.
Victor J. Medina, Founder of Palante Wealth Advisors, solved this inside the AI Business Lab® Mastermind.
“The AI Business Lab® Mastermind transformed how I onboard and develop talent. I’ve reduced my personal training time by 16+ hours per hire by building AI-driven systems that protect client experience while accelerating team readiness.”
𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘀: 16+ hours of founder time saved per new hire through AI-driven onboarding systems that maintain client experience standards.
For professional services firms looking to scale without sacrificing quality, the AI Business Lab® Mastermind offers frameworks that work. A few spots remain.

🧠 Company Brain #1: Fragmented Knowledge
Most companies already have the knowledge they need. The real challenge is that this knowledge is scattered across documents, emails, user stories and different systems. The biggest risk is the knowledge that exists only in people’s memories.
It is difficult to search, impossible to scale and easy to lose when someone changes teams or leaves the company.
A Company Brain could connect these fragmented sources through a shared intelligence layer. It should do more than search for matching documents. It should understand the context of a question, identify relevant sources and explain where the answer came from.
This could make onboarding easier, reduce repeated work and preserve knowledge when people change teams or leave the company.
But connecting everything creates an important question: who should be allowed to access what?
That will be the focus of Company Brain #2.
#CompanyBrain #EnterpriseAI #ArtificialIntelligence

🚀 **The 5 AI Agents Every Company Should Implement NOW!** 🚀
As we dive deeper into AI transformations at Section, I've noticed a proven pattern: there are five key agents that consistently show up across industries and company sizes. They don’t require complex engineering or extensive vendor conversations, but they do hinge on one crucial decision: connecting your company data to a large language model (LLM).
Here’s why you should consider implementing these agents:
1. **Chief of Staff**: This agent becomes your personal assistant, triaging your calendar and communications to highlight what needs your attention. At just $75/month/employee, it’s a game changer for productivity!
2. **Meeting Debrief**: It captures key decisions made in meetings, creating a foundational knowledge graph that empowers your team to take informed action.
3. **Weekly Status Writer**: Tired of inconsistent updates? This agent compiles a cohesive weekly summary from various sources, saving valuable time and ensuring clarity across the board.
4. **Call Prep**: Elevate your conversations! This agent organizes context before external meetings, helping you enter discussions fully prepared, turning potential gaps into opportunities.
5. **New Hire Setup**: Smooth out onboarding by providing new team members with essential context, connections, and resources tailored to their role. It’s your strategic asset for maximizing early impact!
✨ **Why these five?** They have a small blast radius and can be easily reversed if needed, making them low-risk. Plus, they leverage existing data and workflows, creating structured records that fuel continued growth.
💡 My recommendation? Start by picking two agents to implement this week, roll out the others next week, and watch the momentum build!

𝗜𝘁 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗺𝗲 𝟯𝟬 𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝘄𝗼 𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗸𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗲𝗳 𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗼𝗳 𝗺𝘆 𝘀𝗼𝗼𝗻-𝘁𝗼-𝗯𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗹𝗲𝗲𝘁.
Way longer than I expected.
But then I considered how long it would take to define, recruit, interview, hire, and onboard a human chief of staff.
Thirty hours suddenly didn’t seem so unreasonable.
My chief of staff will be the first member of the digital team I’m building for my AI consulting business—and eventually, the agent responsible for helping orchestrate the others.
Its job is to help me:
* Keep priorities from getting buried
* Track projects, decisions, and follow-ups
* Reduce the mental load of holding everything in my head
* Turn the way I work into repeatable processes
* Coordinate the specialized agents I’ll add to the fleet
I’m building the operational foundation that will help future humans—and agents—do their best work.
What surprised me was how much “hiring” an AI agent resembles hiring a person.
I had to define the role, establish responsibilities, determine what context it needed, create guardrails, and decide what success should look like.
The technology was only part of the work.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘄𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝘁𝗼𝗴𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿—and how this role would fit into a larger system.
My 2nd lesson from building an agent fleet?
𝗗𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗱𝗼.
𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱𝘀 𝗶𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗼𝘄𝗻.
If you were building an agent fleet, which role would you hire first?
Special thanks to AI Build Lab for making this build possible in a compressed timeframe and for the community I’m learning so much from!

"The best people in a company are often trapped by the worst workflows"
I didn't realize this at first.
For years, I thought great companies were built by great people.
And that is true.
But after working closely with different teams, I noticed something strange.
The people with the most experience were often spending the most time doing things that didn't require their experience.
They were not solving difficult problems.
They were searching for information,
Copying data,
Checking documents,
Following up on approvals,
Updating reports,
Connecting systems that were never designed to work together.
What surprised me was this:
These people were not inefficient.
They were doing exactly what the system around them required.
The problem was not the people.
The problem was the way work was designed.
Every company has invisible workflows.
The email thread that contains the real decision.
The Excel file that everyone depends on.
The employee who remembers how things actually work.
The process that exists only because "this is how we have always done it."
And I started asking myself:
What happens when the person who knows everything leaves?
What happens when the company grows faster than its processes?
What happens when talented people spend more time managing information than creating value?
That question became the beginning of anchor.
I didn't want to build another tool that companies have to learn.
I wanted to help companies rethink how work happens.
Because the future of work is not about asking people to work harder.
It is about removing the unnecessary friction that prevents them from doing their best work.
At Anchor, we believe:
Better businesses are built on better workflows.
We study how teams actually work, identify where friction exists, and redesign the processes behind the work.
Not more complexity.
Not more tools.
Just better ways of working.
This is the beginning of our journey.
I’m excited to share what we learn along the way.
What is one process in your company that feels harder than it should be?

This book, first published in 1989, outlines seven habits that are designed to help individuals become more effective in their personal and professional lives.
The habits are grouped into three categories: Private Victory (habits 1-3), Public Victory (habits 4-6), and Renewal (habit 7).
The habits include being proactive, beginning with the end in mind, putting first things first, thinking win-win, seeking first to understand and then to be understood, synergizing, and sharpening the saw.
Covey emphasizes the importance of personal integrity, effective time management, empathetic communication, and continuous self-improvement.
If your business is taking over your life, it’s time to step back and rethink the playbook. Success shouldn’t come at the cost of everything else. The good news is, it doesn’t have to—and I’m the living proof.
In this episode, the tables are turned as I take the guest seat on Michael Hyatt and Megan Hyatt-Miller’s podcast, The Double Win. We dive into my journey of building Triad Partners—the company I co-founded to help independent financial advisors grow their businesses without losing sight of what really matters.
We cover everything from transitioning from a sales-driven mindset to a CEO role, to the importance of therapy for high-achieving entrepreneurs, to why business culture will make or break your success.
I hope this conversation gives you practical insights and fresh perspectives to help you break free from the hustle trap.
3 of the biggest insights from Brad Johnson & Michael Hyatt …
#1.) Breaking Free from the Hustle Hamster Wheel
Many financial advisors build a business only to find themselves working more hours than ever. We talk about the common cycle of “market, sell, repeat” and how to escape it by structuring your business to scale beyond you.
#2.) The Mindset Shift from Salesperson to CEO
Scaling a business isn’t just about bringing in more clients—it’s about shifting from a doer to a leader. I share the biggest leadership lessons I’ve learned while growing Triad from the ground up and building a 100-person team in just four years.
#3.) Culture Is Everything
Hiring the best talent is important, but if they’re not a culture fit, they’ll do more harm than good. We break down how Triad built a movement around Do Business, Do Life and why culture is the ultimate competitive advantage.

Serial tech entrepreneurs who have built successful companies time and again have deep knowledge and expertise. The most dangerous word in AI right now: “free.”
OpenClaw is open source. Free to download. But every action it takes burns API tokens—and the costs are staggering.
• One blogger: $3,600/month in token costs
• One user: $200 burned in a single day from a looping task
• My experience: $600 in four days
The tool ships with no spending caps, no budget alerts, and no circuit breakers. If something goes wrong, the meter runs until your credit hits zero.
As one analysis noted: token costs regularly exceed what you’d pay a human executive assistant at $50/hour.
For most SMB leaders, the math doesn’t work. Not yet.

This week, I asked an LLM to multiply two large numbers: 2837 × 4853. It gave me an answer: confident, and incorrect.
So I followed up. “Are you sure?” I asked. It responded again, equally confident, and this time, thankfully also correct.
That exchange explains more about AI systems than most product demos.
Traditional software is deterministic. The same set of inputs produces the identical output, every single time. LLMs are probabilistic. They do not calculate in the way a calculator does. They predict the most likely sequence of tokens based on training data.
Change the phrasing slightly, and you can change the outcome. That flexibility is what makes them powerful. It is also what makes them unreliable in contexts where precision is non-negotiable.
For investors, the real question is not whether a company is “AI native,” it is understanding how reliability is engineered into the system. Where are errors caught? Which parts of the solution are deterministic, which are probabilistic? What happens when the model is wrong?
I explore this in depth in my latest blog - follow the link in the comments.

#Why_Adding_More_Tools_Make_Your_Agent_Worse?
Unbelievable fact about AI agents:
Adding more tools makes them worse.
Here's why.
Every tool definition consumes context window space.
Each tool needs a description, input schema, output schema,
and usage guidance. That's stable, predictable space,
but it adds up fast.
Give an agent 50 tools and you've burned thousands of tokens
before a single user message arrives.
But the real problem isn't space. It's decision quality.
The more tools an agent has, the harder it is to choose
the right one. Vague tool descriptions lead to wrong invocations.
Overlapping tools create ambiguity. The LLM starts guessing.
The engineering principle:
→ Every tool description should answer 4 questions:
What does it do?
What inputs does it require, in what format?
What does it return?
When should the agent prefer this tool over alternatives?
If you can't answer all four clearly,
the tool isn't ready for production.
Fewer tools, better described, beat
many tools, poorly documented. Every time.

Most AI systems assume that once an action is “approved,” it stays approved.
That assumption breaks the moment the system becomes distributed.
A workflow starts.
An agent proposes an action.
Upstream checks pass.
But before execution:
• permissions change
• state shifts
• another action commits first
• a dependency moves
Now the question isn’t:
“Was this allowed?”
It’s:
“Is this still allowed right now?”
Most systems don’t answer that.
They carry forward earlier decisions and treat them as authority.
That works in static systems.
It fails in real ones.
Because authorization is not authority at execution.
Authority has to be re-derived against the state that actually exists when the system attempts to act.
If it isn’t, you get:
• time-of-check vs time-of-use gaps
• race-condition-driven behavior
• actions executing against invalid assumptions
The system didn’t “fail policy.”
It executed without re-validating reality.
If your system proposes state transitions:
Where is that re-validation happening?
And what prevents a previously valid action from becoming invalid before it commits?

The evolution of LLMs is pushing a new way of building software. We’ll increasingly see models generating a large portion of the code, while humans move into roles more focused on reviewing, guiding, and deciding.

A quiet truth about today's AI tools: your memory doesn't travel.
What you teach ChatGPT stays in OpenAI's ecosystem. What you build in Claude stays with Anthropic. Gemini operates apart from both. There is no clean way to move your accumulated context between them.
For an individual, that's friction. For a business, it's a strategic liability. Data portability determines whether you can access, export, and reuse the knowledge that powers your operation, outside any single vendor's system. It is the most fundamental dimension of AI risk, and it's the one most leaders overlook.
The fix isn't to bet on the "right" platform. It's to stop depending on any one of them.
Keep your core knowledge, your context, your processes, your reference material, in an open, portable format that you own. Then let whichever model you prefer read from it. The model becomes a tool you can replace. The knowledge remains an asset you keep.
This is the difference between building on rented land and building on ground you own. One leaves you exposed to someone else's roadmap. The other puts you in control.
As AI becomes central to how your organization runs, portability stops being a technical detail and becomes a board-level question.

"Use AI" is the emptiest instruction in corporate right now.
It sounds like direction. What it actually does is hand someone a logo and a deadline, then walk away from every hard decision — which tool, which task, where the risk sits, how the work itself has to change.

Everyone's talking about AI miracles these days. But step out of the tech-news hype and into actual organizational meetings, and you'll quickly discover the real bottleneck isn't AI at all.
We're trying to deploy the most advanced language models on top of systems where:
Data is still recorded manually in notebooks or scattered spreadsheets
Departments refuse to share information with each other (data silos)
Core business processes were never documented they live only in one person's head.
Here's the uncomfortable truth: AI is not a magic wand you wave over messy data and broken processes to produce pure gold.
If your data is fragmented, low-quality, and has no clear ownership and your processes lack transparency even the best AI models won't perform miracles.
Before worrying about whether ChatGPT will replace us, we should be asking: Do our databases meet basic standards? Does our organization actually have a data-driven culture?

Eliminate Developer Dependency Tax with Vibe Coding
This title was summarized by AI from the post below.
Michael Hyatt
7mo
Report this post
Let's talk about what I call the developer dependency tax—the hidden costs of relying on outside development teams.
The financial cost is obvious. Even modest projects typically require $50,000-$200,000 in development fees, with ongoing maintenance costs that never stop.
But the real tax isn't financial. It's operational:
• Every change requires explaining your vision to someone who doesn't live in your business
• Every iteration takes weeks instead of hours
• Every pivot means renegotiating scope and budget
• You're constrained by someone else's availability and understanding
According to McKinsey research, 46% of companies now report significant productivity impact from AI implementation, with many specifically citing reduced dependency on traditional development resources.
Vibe coding eliminates this tax entirely.
You describe what you want. AI builds it. Something doesn't work? You adjust your description and regenerate. No tickets, no sprints, no waiting for the next build cycle.
This shift represents more than cost savings. It's about strategic agility. The ability to move at the speed of your vision rather than your development team's schedule creates a fundamental competitive advantage.
I've experienced both sides: the frustration of waiting weeks for changes that should take hours, and the freedom of iterating on applications in real time.
For business leaders building software-enabled services, this transition from dependency to self-reliance changes everything.
The question is: are you ready to make that shift?
Learn how to eliminate your developer dependency tax: https://lnkd.in/e8p9A35R

Tax planning is one of the highest value services a financial advisor can offer. It is also the most operationally painful.
Usually, it involves requesting PDF tax returns, manually keying data into planning software, and cross referencing paystubs against custodial data. It is slow, mentally draining, and prone to error.
This week, Altruist flipped this dynamic with their new AI platform, Hazel.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺: 𝗜𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹. Hazel does not just calculate numbers. It reads the unstructured mess of a client’s financial life. It ingests 1040 forms, paystubs, account statements, and even meeting notes and emails.
It applies deep tax logic to this unstructured data in minutes, eliminating the manual data entry that typically bottlenecks firms during tax season.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗛𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗟𝗼𝗼𝗽: 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴. The real innovation here isn't the speed; it is the interactivity.
Instead of an advisor taking a week to generate a static report, they can now sit with a client and run live "what if" scenarios.
- What happens if we sell the vacation home?
- What is the tax impact of this year's bonus?
- How does a retirement transition change the liability?
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝘂𝗽𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗮𝘅 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲.
𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀: This keeps the human advisor in the loop but shifts their role. They stop being a data entry clerk and start being a true strategist. As Altruist CEO Jason Wenk noted, this technology "makes average advice a lot harder to justify."
𝗔 𝗡𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗰𝘆: For the Human Loop to work in finance, trust is non negotiable. Hazel operates on a zero data retention agreement. The model providers are prohibited from retaining client data or using it to train their models.
This is the blueprint for vertical AI: Automate the reading, accelerate the math, and let the human handle the judgment.

Why Spreadsheets still dominate Direct Tax Provisioning in AI enabled Finance world and Why that should change:
There’s a behavioral reality few transformation programs truly address:
“Spreadsheets feel safe.”
They are:
🔹flexible when last-minute changes hit
🔹transparent to the person who built them
🔹familiar after years of close cycles and audits
Under tight reporting timelines, leaders hesitate to disrupt a model that “works.”
But here’s the irony. Manual spreadsheet environments are exactly where financial reporting and SOX risk concentrates, relying heavily on human judgment, offline evidence, version control, and compensating controls.
They may survive audits. They rarely scale well.
And they carry significant key-person dependency.
In an AI-enabled Finance world, this fragility becomes increasingly unsustainable.
How Finance transformation roadmaps sideline Tax:
Most Finance transformations start where transaction volume is highest:
🔹Procure to Pay
🔹Order to Cash
🔹Record to Report
Tax provisioning often appears later as “Phase 2” or “Wave 3.”
In reality, those phases are usually the first to be delayed, descoped, or quietly dropped when budgets tighten, priorities shift, or program teams change.
And so, the paradox persists:
Direct tax provisioning is:
🔹time-critical in the close
🔹central to financial statement integrity
🔹heavily judgement-laden
🔹highly scrutinized by audit
Yet it remains one of the least industrialized Finance processes.
The shift that’s coming:
The slow adoption of tax provision engines is not a technology failure.
It reflects how hard it is to synchronize:
process, data, systems, judgment, and governance across Finance and Tax.
But as:
🔹cloud ERPs mature
🔹data platforms stabilize
🔹AI-driven Finance accelerates
the cost of spreadsheet-based provisioning will become harder to justify not just in effort, but in:
🔹control risk
🔹close cycle pressure
🔹scalability
🔹audit defensibility
🔹talent dependency
The leadership question should be changing:
From:
“Should we automate Direct tax provisioning?”
To:
“When will our foundations be strong enough to automate it safely, at scale, and with confidence?”
That’s where modern Finance transformation will quietly distinguish the leaders.

It’s happening.

Set up revenue rules properly.
Build guardrails around automation.
Review the output.
The cleanups I see later are always more expensive than the setup would have been.
The future isn’t no-accountant.
It’s smarter systems
tighter controls
better advisors who know how to use the tools.
AI doesn’t replace judgment.
It amplifies whatever structure you built underneath it.

In the 1980s, powerful desktop computers were going to eliminate accountants.
In the 1990s, advanced tax software was going to do it.
Then the internet was going to make us irrelevant.
Here we are.
Every single time, the professionals who thrived were the ones who picked up the new technology — and used it to become indispensable. The ones who resisted? They struggled.
AI is the next chapter of that same story.
Here's what I tell my colleagues:
**AI won't replace CPAs. But CPAs who use AI will replace those who don't.**
There are three places where this matters most right now:
**1. Your own practice.** AI handles first drafts, research, correspondence, and document review in a fraction of the time. The solo practitioner who embraces this works like a team of three.
**2. Your staff.** When your team stops spending their days on mechanical tasks, they contribute at a higher level sooner. That's better for clients, better for morale, and better for your bottom line.
**3. Your advisory capacity.** AI can process data fast. What it can't do is look a business owner in the eye and tell them their current path isn't working. That judgment, that relationship, that trust — that's yours. Protect it by freeing up more time for it.
Some accounting work is genuinely at risk — rote data entry, commodity returns, basic bookkeeping done the same way it's always been done. But the practitioners most at risk aren't in the wrong field. They're clinging to the wrong model.
The window to get ahead of this is open right now.
What are you doing to future-proof your practice?

There's a risk embedded in most AI implementations that rarely appears in the vendor pitch: knowledge lock-in.
As AI tools accumulate context about your business—your voice, your preferences, your workflows—that context becomes embedded in the platform. Switching becomes increasingly expensive. Not just in migration costs, but in the loss of compounded context that took months to build.
The risk isn't that you chose the wrong model—models are improving quickly, and what's optimal today may not be in twelve months. The risk is that your knowledge isn't portable.
The mitigation is structural: store your knowledge in formats you own, independent of the AI platform. Plain text files, local notes, portable databases. Your knowledge should be separable from whatever model or platform is currently processing it.
This isn't an argument against committing to a platform. Consolidating your AI stack on one platform is still the right operational move for most executives—it's the only way to accumulate the contextual depth that makes AI genuinely powerful.
The distinction is between the platform (which can change) and the knowledge base (which should travel with you). Organizations that architect for portability now will have significantly more flexibility as the AI landscape continues to shift.

The hard part of enterprise AI is not proving that the tool can do something useful.
Most teams have already proved that.
The hard part is turning useful experiments into reliable operations.
That shift changes the work.
An AI experiment can live inside a sandbox, a demo, or a motivated team.
AI-enabled operations need something more durable:
- a named workflow owner
- clear data and system boundaries
- approval gates for high-impact decisions
- exception paths when confidence drops
- audit trails for what happened and why
- metrics tied to cycle time, quality, risk, or capacity
This is where many enterprise AI programs stall.
They move from tool adoption to tool sprawl without redesigning the operating layer around the work.
For leaders planning AI initiatives this quarter, I would use a simple filter before scaling the next pilot:
Can the team explain how this workflow will run on a normal Tuesday?
Who reviews the output?
Who can override the system?
What evidence is logged?
Where does human judgment remain mandatory?
What metric proves the workflow improved?
If those answers are vague, the organization may not have an AI capability yet.
It has an AI experiment with production ambitions.
The path forward is not slower AI adoption.
It is better operational design.
Readiness first.
Governance second.
Workflow redesign third.
Then scale the AI.

The most important consequence of cheaper AI is not lower cost. It is what lower cost makes possible.
The conventional assumption is that as models become cheaper and more open, demand for AI infrastructure will decline.
History suggests the opposite.
When storage became cheaper, companies stored more data. When bandwidth became cheaper, video consumption exploded. As AI inference becomes cheaper, enterprises will not simply spend less to perform the same tasks. They will embed intelligence into far more workflows and run it far more often.
That changes the enterprise AI equation.
In healthcare, lower inference costs could move AI from answering an occasional question to continuously helping people navigate eligibility, benefits, provider networks, medications, care options, and next actions.
That does not reduce infrastructure requirements. It expands them.
More importantly, it increases the value of the system surrounding the models:
• Permissioned data
• Identity and consent
• Governance and escalation
• Specialized tools and agents
• Enterprise workflows
• Integrated action pathways
• Measurement and accountability
As models become more accessible, the model itself becomes less of the differentiator.
The advantage moves to the companies that can orchestrate increasingly abundant intelligence inside trusted, working systems.
Cheaper intelligence will not make enterprise AI less valuable. It will make intelligence ubiquitous and raise the value of everything required to put it to work.

If you cannot explain what your AI did, you do not have a production system.
You have a demonstration.
Enterprise AI Blueprint #011 | AI Observability
Many AI teams focus heavily on whether the final answer is accurate.
But in an enterprise environment, accuracy alone is not enough.
You also need to understand:
• Which data and context were used?
• Which model, agent and tools were involved?
• What actions were taken?
• Which policies and permissions were applied?
• Where did human intervention occur?
• Can the entire decision be reconstructed?
This becomes even more important with Agentic AI.
A chatbot may produce one response.
An AI agent can retrieve information, call tools, update systems and trigger downstream actions.
Without end-to-end observability, organisations may see the outcome, but have no reliable way to explain how it was produced.
Enterprise AI observability should therefore cover more than infrastructure health.
It should provide visibility across the complete decision pipeline:
→ Context
→ Retrieval
→ Reasoning
→ Tool calls
→ Actions
→ Outcome
And it should connect technical telemetry with business impact.
Not only:
“Did the workflow complete?”
But also:
“Was the right decision made, under the right constraints, at an acceptable cost?”
Because when AI moves into production, trust depends on more than performance.
It depends on whether the organisation can observe, explain and govern what the system is doing.
Could your organisation reconstruct an AI-driven decision six months after it was made?

Most leaders treat their AI tools as software. The smarter ones are starting to treat them as infrastructure, and infrastructure decisions carry risk.
Gartner has warned that enterprises going all-in on a single AI provider create a deep dependency that erodes their technical agility and their negotiating power on price, terms, and service. That's not a minor inconvenience. It's a structural commitment that gets harder to unwind every month.
Here's what most teams miss. The lock-in isn't only at the model layer. It's in your data, your workflows, and the institutional knowledge your people have poured into one platform. The longer you stay, the deeper it runs.
What's true for the Fortune 500 is just as true for a 15-person company. When your knowledge, your models, and your workflows all live inside one vendor's walls, that vendor sets the rules and you live with them.
The mitigation is straightforward in principle: keep the asset that matters most, your knowledge, in a portable form you control, and treat the model as a swappable component.
The organizations that will scale AI safely are the ones designing for portability now, before the dependency is too expensive to exit.
I unpack the three shifts that make this practical here:

Vendors are exceptionally good at one thing:
Making their solution feel like your problem's answer.
This isn't criticism. It's their job. They present with precision, they benchmark across industries, and they arrive with evidence that's hard to argue with in a room.
The structural problem is what happens after the meeting.
Organizations with strong internal AI ownership walk out asking: does this solve our actual problem?
Organizations over-indexed on vendor relationships walk out asking: how do we implement this?
That single difference in question determines whether AI investment builds capability or complexity.
Vendors operate across clients. They bring breadth. What they can't bring is the one thing that determines whether any solution actually works at your scale — accountability for the outcome after the contract is signed.
That accountability lives internally. Or it lives nowhere.
The most expensive AI decisions I've seen weren't bad technology choices. They were good technology choices for someone else's problem, adopted because the demo was compelling and the internal evaluation process hadn't happened yet.
The organizations building genuine AI advantage have one thing in common: they define the problem internally before any external conversation begins.
The vendor should answer your question.
Not write it.
Where does vendor influence end and internal AI strategy begin in your organization — and is that line clearly drawn?

Choosing an AI vendor is harder than choosing the technology.
Here are the 5 questions that filter out the noise fast.
Choosing an AI vendor is harder than choosing the technology.
Here are the 5 questions that filter out the noise fast.
After running dozens of these conversations, this is the short list I'd hand any business owner before they sign anything.
1. 'Show me a business like mine that you've helped.'
Vague case studies are a red flag. You want a specific example, with specific numbers, and ideally a phone number for the client.
2. 'What's the smallest version of this we can ship in 30 days?'
Anyone insisting on a 6-month build before showing value is selling you risk, not progress. Good partners can carve out a tight pilot.
3. 'What happens to the data, and who owns it?'
If they can't answer in plain language, they haven't thought about it, or they're hoping you don't ask.
4. 'What does the handover look like at the end?'
Will your team be able to maintain it? Or are you locked into them forever? Both can be valid, but you need to know which one you're signing up for.
5. 'What's the failure scenario?'
Every honest partner will tell you what could go wrong. If they say nothing can go wrong, run.
These five questions take ten minutes. They will save you months and a lot of money.
Most vendors won't fail on the technology. They'll fail on these.

We are kicking off CDL-Paris 2025–2026 with Michael Hyatt. And we couldn’t have asked for a better start!
Michael is Founding Partner of Creative Destruction Lab, serial entrepreneur, Executive Chair and co-founder of BlueCat, CBC News Network commentator, and Dragon's Den investor—set the tone for an ambitious year (and many more).

What impresses me most is the diversity and quality of this ecosystem around founders and mentors. ~112 ventures are starting the program this year, each bringing a scientific solution for the betterment of humankind, lives-backed by outstanding mentors, serial entrepreneurs and investors like Michael, plus scientists, professors, students, and business professionals.

Conquer the Chaos: Goal Setting to Score Your “Life Goals” with the Double Win with Michael Hyatt
In this episode of Conquer the Chaos, Michael Hyatt, founder and chairman of Full Focus, joins Clate Mask to explore the concept of achieving the "double win" in life, balancing success in work and personal life. Together they explore practical strategies for goal setting, introducing the "SMARTER" framework emphasizing specificity, measurability, excitement, and risk, while acknowledging the crucial role of emotion in goal attainment.
Transcript
Welcome to Conquer the Chaos where entrepreneurs share real stories of how they mastered their own chaos and found success. Host Clate Mask takes you behind the scenes to hear the tough lessons learned so you don't repeat them. These are the stories you don't hear every day.
Clate Mask (00:27):
Welcome everyone to this episode of the Conquer the Chaos podcast. I am Clate Mask, your co-host and CEO of Keap, and I'm so excited today to bring to you someone with great wisdom that is going to help you conquer the chaos and in particular, practice the three personal keys to success. I'm going to now welcome Michael Hyatt. Thank you so much, Michael, for being with us.
Michael Hyatt (00:50):
Clate, thanks for having me.
Clate Mask (00:51):
You bet. Thanks so much. I would love for the audience to get a little bit of a taste of who you are. You and I have begun, have gotten closer here in the past year or so, but in the past we've had a relationship from a business standpoint with your usage of Keap, and then more recently you've joined our advisory board and we've gotten to know each other and I've loved and just thrilled at how the three personal keys to success that we talk about and conquer the chaos fit so well with what you teach. Why don't you take just a minute and share with our audience a little bit about you and what you and your company teach.
Michael Hyatt (01:27):
Well, thank you. We believe in something called the Double Win and that everybody deserves to have the double win, which is to win at work and succeed at life. So many business owners are willing, or at least it seems this way, that they're willing to sacrifice everything for the success of their business. It's not unusual to meet people that have got a very successful business, but have a very toxic marriage or their health is falling apart or their most important relationships are in trouble. That doesn't have to be true. No, it requires some planning and it requires making some decisions, but it can be done. In terms of me, I've been married for 46 years to my first wife and we have five grown daughters, we have 10 grandchildren and all of them live within 20 minutes of us, and the 10 grandkids live within five minutes of us.
Michael Hyatt (02:24):
That's been a lot of fun and we make our family really a priority. There's a time in the past when I didn't make it a priority and it's how I got to the double win was because I was one of those guys that was killing it at work. Meanwhile, my family is suffering, my health is suffering everything else, but our business is called Full focus and basically we're committed to helping people get the double win. Until we get together next time, everybody keep growing and make sure that you are focusing on that double win as Michael Hyatt says, thanks everybody. Take care.

Michael Hyatt founded BlueCat, which was sold for over $700M. Since then he’s shifted to the investor side and has invested in dozens of startups. He shares several insights on what it’s like to be a founder and investor through these storms. Founders should pay attention. Send me a message to let me know what you think!

BlueCat Networks raises $16.8 million
July 22, 2011
BlueCat Networks, an IPAM Intelligence company, announced
the completion of a $16.8 million round of financing by new investor Trident
Capital.
With this investment, the company will continue to
develop, sell and support the market’s most-innovative IP Address Management,
DNS and DHCP solutions. BlueCat Networks will use the funding primarily to
support the expansion of its Sales and Engineering teams and the further
development of its global channel partner program.
Trident Capital managing director J. Alberto Yepez joins
the BlueCat Networks
Board of Directors.
BlueCat Networks has enjoyed remarkable success in the
DNS, DHCP and IP Address Management market and the demand for our solutions
continues to grow,” said Michael Hyatt, co-founder and CEO, BlueCat Networks.
This new funding will enable us to continue to invest in
the quality people, innovation and industry partnerships that drive our
achievements, while maintaining a cash reserve for future
opportunities. We welcome Trident Capital as an investor and valued member
of our team and thank them for supporting our vision,” Hyatt added.
Trident Capital has
an exceptional track record of building successful infrastructure software
companies including: Bytemobile, Epicor mBlox, Merchant eSolutions, Qualys,
Signio, Sygate), Tablus Thor Technologies, and Tricipher.
For the past 18 years, Trident Capital has focused on
investing in entrepreneurs and innovators that are setting the direction of
their respective markets,” said J. Alberto Yepez, managing director, Trident
Capital.
BlueCat Networks is a leader in the IP Address Management
market with proven solutions implemented by a growing base of satisfied
customers and channel partners worldwide. The growth of the IPAM market is set
to explode, propelled by key business and technology drivers including the
proliferation of IP-enabled devices, the migration to emerging Internet
technologies like IPv6, the growing need to secure network infrastructure by
implementing standards like DNSSEC and the requirement for regulatory
compliance.

Building a Business that Lasts
Many businesses are started every day, but the number that lasts the test of time is much lower. So what separates the businesses that last and those that don't? With this podcast, we intend to find out. Each week, we'll feature conversations with business owners who have lasted the test of time to gather stories, tips, and ideas, that will help others grow.

Transcript
What does it take to build a business that lasts—without losing yourself or your family along the way?
Michael Hyatt, bestselling author, speaker, and business leader, joins Jay Owen to share his journey of turning around companies, setting boundaries, and creating a life of intentional success. From leading as CEO of Thomas Nelson Publishers to building Full Focus with his daughter as CEO, Michael has lived out the “double win”—winning at work and at home.
In this episode, you’ll learn:
Why most people “drift” through life—and how to design yours with intention
The turning point that helped Michael redefine success and protect his family
Practical ways to set boundaries that create freedom, not constraints
How to navigate parenting through every season, from kids to adults
Where AI fits in business and life—and how to use it without losing your humanity
Michael’s story proves that lasting success isn’t about working more hours—it’s about leading yourself first, setting clear boundaries, and building a legacy that matters.
Learn more about Michael’s work at https://fullfocus.co and his new AI newsletter at https://aibusinesslab.ai.

The most common mistake I observe in executive AI adoption isn't choosing the wrong tool. It's choosing too many.
The pattern is familiar: one tool for email drafting, another for research, a third for meeting summaries, a fourth for scheduling, a fifth for reporting. Each solves a specific problem adequately. Together, they create a new one.
Context doesn't travel between disconnected tools. Every system starts fresh. The preferences, history, and institutional knowledge that make AI genuinely useful accumulate nowhere.
The result is that AI stays at the level of a capable assistant you have to re-orient every day—rather than becoming the operational backbone of the business.
The solution is structural: build your entire AI delegation stack on one platform. Both modes—on-demand requests and scheduled automations—running from a single interface, accumulating context in one location.
When the stack is consolidated, the gains compound. Each successive automation is easier to configure, outputs are more contextually accurate, and the knowledge base that powers the whole system grows with every interaction.
This is the fourth step in the delegation framework I've outlined for CEOs: list the tasks, sort them, delegate three a week, consolidate the stack.
The full twelve-task framework and platform guidance are in this week's newsletter:
