Most companies don’t have an AI problem.
They have an execution problem.
Organizations are buying AI licences.
Launching copilots.
Running proof-of-concepts.
Creating innovation teams.
But few are converting those experiments into enterprise-wide productivity.
Why?
Because AI adoption is being treated as a technology rollout—not a business transformation.
The five barriers I see repeatedly are:
1. No clear business-value priorities
Teams pursue interesting AI ideas instead of solving high-cost, high-volume or high-friction business problems.
Fix: Select 3–5 use cases with clear owners, baselines and measurable outcomes.
---
2. Fragmented AI governance
Different functions use different tools, duplicate initiatives and expose confidential data without adequate oversight.
Fix: Establish approved tools, data rules, risk classifications, human review and accountable use-case owners.
---
3. Poor data and knowledge readiness
AI cannot produce dependable answers when enterprise information is outdated, duplicated, inaccessible or poorly controlled.
Fix: Build a trusted knowledge layer around the selected use cases—not the entire organization at once.
---
4. Low workforce adoption
Buying licences does not change behaviour.
Generic AI training rarely translates into daily productivity.
Fix: Create role-specific workflows, prompt libraries, AI champions and weekly adoption metrics.
---
5. AI layered over broken processes
Automating an inefficient process only makes inefficiency move faster.
Fix: Eliminate unnecessary work, simplify approvals, automate rules and use AI where human judgement must be augmented.
---
The near-term CXO agenda should be simple:
✅ Identify the highest-value work
✅ Redesign the underlying process
✅ Deploy AI within controlled workflows
✅ Train employees around actual roles
✅ Measure hours, cost, quality and cycle time
✅ Scale what works—and stop what does not
The organizations that win with AI will not be those with the most pilots.
They will be those that build the strongest system for turning AI into measurable business outcomes.
Where is your organization today: experimenting, adopting or scaling?

Where is your organization on the AI maturity journey? 📊
Most companies treat AI adoption like an on/off switch. In reality, it happens in distinct stages. Skipping stages is usually why transformation stalls. You can't scale enterprise value on top of weak governance or fragmented data.
Across the market today, these are the 4 stages of AI maturity most organizations navigate:
⚡ Stage 1: Everyday AI (Personal Productivity)
- What it looks like: Employees using tools like ChatGPT or Copilots individually to write faster, summarize meetings, and draft code.
- Recommended focus: AI Literacy & Guardrails. Define clear usage policies so employees build habits safely without risking data privacy.
⚙️ Stage 2: Process-Embedded AI (Workflow Integration)
- What it looks like: AI embedded directly into day-to-day software to automate routine tasks (e.g., invoice processing or CRM updates).
- Recommended focus: Data Quality & Process Redesign. Clean your data pipelines and redesign workflows around human-AI collaboration before adding more tools.
🚀 Stage 3: Scaled Enterprise AI (Agentic Automation)
- What it looks like: Autonomous AI agents handling complex, cross-functional tasks across multiple business units.
- Recommended focus: Governance, ROI & Cost Control. Shift from tracking "time saved" to measuring hard P&L impact, risk controls, and running costs.
💡 Stage 4: Transformational AI (New Business Models)
- What it looks like: AI driving the core operating model to create brand-new products, services, and revenue streams.
- Recommended focus: Strategic Alignment. Keep executive leadership aligned on reinventing business models as technology evolves.
Moving up this curve isn't about buying more AI tools, it's about building the internal capability to capture and measure value at every level.
💡 Where is your organization on this journey today? Are you driving quick productivity wins in Stage 1, or scaling cross-functional impact in Stage 3? Let’s connect in the comments! 👇

Everyone got faster. Almost nobody can prove it.
That's the most uncomfortable number in business this year:
89% of executives say AI has increased the speed of work, but only 6% can point to measurable, organisation-wide ROI.
I don't think that gap is a technology problem. It's a measurement problem, and a workflow one.
Three things I keep seeing behind it:
We measure adoption, not outcomes. Seat counts and usage dashboards are easy. Cycle time, error rates, and cost per output are the ones that matter.
Speed backs up at the human gates. When drafting gets 5x faster but review, approval, and QA don't, the queue just moves downstream.
Volume isn't value. Output that someone else has to decipher and redo isn't productivity, it's cost with better formatting.
The organisations pulling ahead did something unglamorous: they picked one high-frequency workflow, gave one person authority to redesign it end to end, and measured a financial outcome not a usage stat.
Which is why 20% of organisations are now capturing 74% of AI's economic value.
The 6% isn't a verdict on the technology. It's a to-do list.

US$30–40 billion has already been poured into AI by enterprises.
That’s roughly the annual R&D budget of a major tech giant — 𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝟑𝟎 𝐭𝐨 𝟒𝟎 𝐁𝐮𝐫𝐣 𝐊𝐡𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐚𝐬.
And the spending is only going up.
Yet here’s the uncomfortable part:
95% of AI pilots are failing to scale or deliver meaningful P&L impact.
Why?
Because too many boards still treat AI as a technology project.
Usually with a narrow question:
“How do we do this cheaper?”
But the better question is:
“𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐧𝐨𝐰?”
AI success is not just about model quality.
It is about leadership judgment.
The winning enterprises are not using AI merely to reduce headcount.
They are using it to multiply capability.
But many organizations fall into three traps:
1. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐍𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐰 𝐀𝐈 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐩
Automating isolated tasks, creating brittle specialists instead of adaptive systems.
2. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐩
Trying to make AI replace humans, instead of augmenting human judgment, creativity and speed.
3. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐏&𝐋 𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧

AI pilots don’t need to take six months to prove value.
For operations leaders, the real opportunity is to move from AI curiosity to measurable business impact quickly, safely, and with discipline.
A practical 30-day AI pilot can help teams validate whether AI actually improves a workflow before investing in broader rollout.
The key is not to start with the biggest or most complex use case.
It is to identify 3–5 high-leverage, low-risk opportunities where teams are already spending significant time on repetitive, predictable work.
Here’s what a focused 30-day roadmap can look like:
🔹 Week 1: Define and select
Map repetitive tasks, score them based on value and risk, choose 2–3 strong candidates, and set a clear business goal.
The most important guardrail: AI suggests, humans decide.
🔹 Week 2: Configure and prepare
Assign ownership, create a small cross-functional team, define data privacy guardrails, and establish success metrics before building or testing anything.
Metrics should focus on business outcomes such as cycle time, error reduction, cost savings, or decision quality.
🔹 Week 3: Run the pilot
Test the workflow 10–15 times in a real or sandbox environment.
Capture clear “before vs. after” evidence.
Train human reviewers to know when to approve, escalate, or reject AI recommendations.
🔹 Week 4: Review and validate
Compare pilot results against the baseline.
Then make a clear decision:
✅ Scale if the value is stable and repeatable
✅ Fix if the value is promising but the process needs improvement
✅ Drop if adoption or impact is too low
One of the most valuable outputs is a simple 1-page internal case study that shows what was tested, what changed, what was learned, and what business value was created.
This matters because AI adoption is not just a technology challenge.
It is an operations, governance, measurement, and leadership challenge.
The organizations that win with AI will not be the ones that chase every new tool. They will be the ones that build repeatable systems for testing, learning, measuring, and scaling responsibly.
Start small. Measure what matters. Keep humans in the loop. Document the risks. Then scale what works.

“AI is improving productivity…but why is my AI bill growing faster than the value we’re getting?”
That was a question a CXO asked during a business leadership meeting we had. It caught everyone’s attention because it’s a question many organizations are beginning to grapple with.
For the last two years, the conversation has been about AI adoption.
How do we encourage teams to use AI?
How do we embed AI into everyday work?
How do we accelerate productivity?
But as AI moves from pilots to enterprise-wide deployment, a different challenge is emerging.
Cost.
Every prompt, document summary, report, analysis, or code generation consumes tokens. Individually they seem insignificant. Across thousands of employees and millions of interactions, they become a meaningful line item on the P&L.
The instinctive response is often to give everyone access to the most capable AI model.
But that’s similar to asking every employee to travel business class—regardless of whether they’re flying for a routine internal meeting or a critical client negotiation.
The objective isn’t to use the best AI for every task.
It’s to use the right AI for the right task.
Routine work—emails, meeting notes, document summaries, standard reports—can often be handled by smaller, lower-cost models.
Reserve the most advanced models for:
* Strategic analysis
* Complex problem-solving
* Executive decision support
* High-impact customer engagements
Every technology follows a similar maturity curve.
Phase 1: Adoption
Phase 2: Optimization
Phase 3: Governance
I believe we’re now entering Phase 2.
The organizations that will create a sustainable competitive advantage won’t necessarily be those spending the most on AI. They’ll be the ones that build AI governance, model-routing strategies, and cost discipline into their operating model—while continuing to unlock business value.
The next frontier of AI leadership isn’t adoption. It’s AI ROI.
How are you approaching AI today?
* Maximizing usage?
* Or optimizing value per AI dollar spent?

"How should we use AI to scale?"

"What are you trying to sustain?"
Silence.
The conversation changed immediately.
Because most organizations today are obsessed with scaling.
Very few are thinking about sustaining.
As Peter Drucker famously said:
"There is nothing so useless as doing efficiently that which should not be done at all."
AI is becoming the greatest efficiency engine businesses have ever seen.
But efficiency is not strategy.
In boardrooms across industries, I see companies investing in AI, automation, analytics, and digital transformation.
Yet many have not answered some fundamental questions:
- Which capabilities will become irrelevant?
- Which decisions must remain human?
- What makes us different when everyone has access to the same AI?
- What do we want to be known for five years from now?
A weak process automated by AI becomes a faster weak process.
A confused strategy executed through AI becomes a faster route to confusion.
Technology amplifies.
It does not automatically improve.

First, survive.
Protect what matters.
Understand the threats.
Adapt to reality.

Strengthen culture.

What must remain.

Because in business, scale creates visibility.
Sustainability creates longevity.
And longevity creates influence.
Survive. Sustain. Scale.
In that order.

The Most Underrated Canadian Founder You’ve Probably Never Heard Of
If Michael Hyatt were American, he’d have 500,000 LinkedIn followers, a book deal, and a Netflix documentary called “How to Print Money Legally.”
But he’s Canadian…
So nobody talks about him.
Let’s fix that.
Meet Michael Hyatt: the quiet Canadian who sold not one, but TWO huge companies before he turned 30.
Everyone knows Shopify.
Everyone knows Lululemon.
But almost nobody knows the guy who built one of Canada’s most valuable cybersecurity firms and sold it for $400M+, and then just kept going.
This is why I love studying founders like Hyatt:
They aren’t loud.
They aren’t flashy.
They just win.
The Story
At 17, he’s playing with servers while the rest of us were trying to get a date to grad.
At 25, he starts his first tech company, Dyadem.
At 29, he sells it.
Then he does the most un-Canadian thing ever:
He starts another one.
That company?
BlueCat.
The invisible plumbing behind the internet that no one thinks about until it breaks.
Think cybersecurity meets infrastructure meets “oh God don’t let this fail.”
Everyone said building it in Canada was impossible.
Hyatt built it anyway.
Scaled it.
Then sold it for hundreds of millions.
Instead of buying a yacht and disappearing to Anguilla, he becomes an angel investor, backs dozens of companies, becomes a CBC Dragon, gives straight-talk business advice, and mentors founders across the country.
No ego.
No influencer vibes.
Just results.
Why I’m Obsessed With His Playbook
Here’s the thing about Hyatt:
He didn’t build a social app.
He didn’t build a marketplace.
He built boring infrastructure that powers the internet.
And boring infrastructure is where the money is.
His lessons hit hard:
Solve real problems, “not founder feelings.”
Ignore hype, focus on customers who pay.
Build discipline, not dopamine.
Be relentless, even when nobody sees you.
Think decades, not quarters.
Canada desperately needs more founders like him, quiet killers who build important things instead of shiny things.
The Takeaway
Canada has a lot of amazing founders building amazing things.
They’re the ones who don’t go viral.
They don’t chase clout.
They build internet plumbing, cybersecurity rails, utilities, enterprise tools, the stuff billion-dollar companies rely on.
Hyatt is the blueprint:
Start small
Build something real
Sell it
Do it again
Help others
Simple.
Not easy.
If you’re building something in Canada, study this man.
He’s one of our country’s best founders.
We just haven’t built him a statue yet.

Money entered but never stayed.
And I was constantly solving problems that shouldn’t have existed in the first place.
When the business grows faster than the structure behind it,
failure becomes inevitable — no matter how talented you are.
So when I finally got it right — when I built businesses that don’t drain me, businesses that run with clarity and predictability — I realized something important:
If I ever start another business from scratch,
I’m not starting with branding, website, staff, or even the product.
I’m starting with systems.
Because systems determine whether the business survives, grows, or collapses.
Here are the first 5 systems I will put in place before anything else:
1️⃣ Leadership System
To define direction, decision-making, accountability, and culture.
Businesses don’t rise to the level of their goals — they rise to the level of their leadership clarity.
2️⃣ Operations System
So work becomes predictable, repeatable, and consistent.
Operations are the backbone. Without them, even the best ideas become chaos.
3️⃣ Marketing System
Not random posting, not inconsistent ads —
a system that constantly attracts qualified leads without stress or desperation.
4️⃣ Sales System
So conversions don’t rely on “talented salespeople,”
but on a clear, repeatable process that delivers the same result every time.
5️⃣ Finance System
Because a business can be busy and still be broke.
Finance systems protect you from silent failure — the kind you don’t notice until it’s too late.
The truth is:
My first four businesses didn’t fail because I was unlucky.
They failed because I was building energy, not systems.
Now?
I run two thriving businesses, and the difference is night and day.
Not because I became smarter…
but because I became structured.
And whenever I’m ready to build the third,
The systems come first.
How has building systems or lack of it affected your business?

Exit-Ready Without Exiting: Why Every Founder Should Build Like They’re Selling
Most founders I talk to have no plans to sell their business. They’re building for the long haul, maybe passing it to family someday, or just running it profitably for years.
So why do I keep telling them to get “exit ready”?
Because exit readiness isn’t about selling. It’s about building a business that runs without you constantly holding it together.
What Exit-Ready Actually Means
An exit-ready business has three things:
- Clean, auditable financials
- Documented systems and processes
- Operations that don’t depend on the founder’s daily presence
These same things make your business more valuable, easier to scale, and frankly, less exhausting to run.
The Real Benefits (Even If You Never Sell)
You can take a vacation. If your business falls apart when you’re unreachable for two weeks, you don’t own a business you own a job.
You can raise capital. Banks and investors want to see proper financials and documented processes. Whether you need equipment financing or growth capital, exit-ready businesses get better terms.
You can hire senior talent. Good executives want to join companies with real systems, not just founder intuition and “we’ll figure it out.”
You have options. Life changes. Health issues happen. Family priorities shift. An exit-ready business gives you flexibility to step back, bring in a partner, or yes sell if circumstances change.
Where to Start
Get your books clean. Personal and business expenses separated. Monthly financial statements you can actually trust. A chart of accounts that makes sense. This isn’t optional, it’s foundational.
Document your processes. The stuff only you know how to do? Write it down. Client onboarding, supplier relationships, quality checks, problem escalation. Start with the things that would break if you were gone.
Build management layers. You don’t need a full C-suite, but you need people who can make decisions without you. This might mean a strong operations manager, a reliable bookkeeper, or a sales lead who owns the pipeline.
Create a real org chart. Even if it’s just five people. Clear roles and reporting lines make it obvious where gaps exist and what needs to change as you grow.
The Test
Ask yourself, “Could someone competent run my business for three months with minimal input from me?”
If not, you’re not exit ready. You’re also probably exhausted.
The Bottom Line
Building an exit-ready business isn’t about planning to leave. It’s about creating something sustainable, scalable, and honestly sane to operate.
You might never sell. But you’ll sleep better knowing you could.

Cleaning up your inner world is a huge business growth lever.
So I turned it into a simple clean-up process I use on repeat.
Most founders don’t think about this.
I didn’t either until I noticed something strange:
my business bottlenecks weren’t operational, they were internal.
I’ve worked with founders at every stage and I’ve watched this pattern repeat:
the ones who scale cleanly aren’t just strategic, they’re emotionally uncluttered.
For me, it showed up quietly.
No big breakdown or dramatic pivot.
No “I moved to Bali and found myself.”
Just this constant low-grade friction.
Decisions took longer than they should.
I second-guessed offers I knew were good.
There was a subtle heaviness around visibility, pricing, and rest.
(Why did raising my rates feel like I was asking for a personal favor?)
So instead of adding another tool, I did something else.
I started clearing.
Not my inbox.
My inner environment.
Much more difficult, but much stickier.
And that’s when things moved.
So I turned it into a framework I now use for myself and with clients:
The Inner Clean-Out Method
☞ Name the leaks
Where does your energy consistently drain?
Look for patterns.
The hesitation before posting. The sigh before client calls.
The resentment you keep justifying.
☞ Separate truth from inheritance
Ask: Did I choose this belief, or did I absorb it?
Urgency culture, rest guilt, fear of being seen. Most of it isn’t yours.
☞ Install boundaries before strategy
Before refining your offer or funnel, decide:
What am I no longer available for?
Misaligned clients love a boundary-free environment.
☞ Clear one internal rule
“I must be liked.”
“I can’t slow down.”
“I need permission.”
Delete one and watch decisions suddenly require fewer Google Docs.
☞ Replace, don’t leave empty
Clearing without replacement creates wobble.
Install something intentional: trust, spaciousness, self-respect, patience.
Chaos will try to move back in if you don’t.
After doing this, here’s what changed:
I decide faster.
My offers feel cleaner.
My pricing feels anchored.
Clients feel easier to say yes to.
Creative momentum returned without force.
I’ve seen the same shift in founders who stop trying to optimize around their internal noise,
and finally address it directly.
Are you avoiding the emotional mess underneath your business?
To your becoming,
Claire Marie ♥

🎁✨With the holidays approaching, I’ve been reflecting on my acquisition search and the types of businesses that truly stand out. The season is a good reminder of how much small businesses mean to their teams and communities - and how important it is to carry that forward in any transition.
The more deals I review, the more I realize something important:
A “great business” isn’t defined by the P&L alone.
The financials matter — of course — but the real indicators show up in the people, the processes, and the pride inside the business.
Here are the things that consistently stand out to me:
1. Long-tenured teams.
People who stay because they trust the owner and take pride in their work. That says more than any KPI.
2. Loyal, recurring customers.
Not transactional. Not chasing volume. Just consistent repeat business built on reliability.
3. Simple, steady operations.
Clear processes. Nothing overly fragile. A business that runs on discipline, not heroics.
4. A reputation that’s been earned, not marketed.
When customers describe the company with words like “reliable,” “fair,” or “honest,” that’s a green flag.
5. An owner who cares about continuity.
The best businesses were built carefully, over years. Those transitions deserve the same care.
After looking at dozens of opportunities, I’ve learned:
A strong balance sheet is important — but character, culture, and consistency are what make a company worth owning.

The most dangerous moment in a new business isn't the launch.
It's month three.
When the initial energy runs out. When the first strategy doesn't work. When you're alone at your laptop realizing nobody taught you this part.
20% of new businesses fail in year one, but the decisions that kill them happen in the first 90 days. Not the big, dramatic ones. The quiet ones.
What to charge. Who to trust. Whether to pivot or push through.
These aren't failures of effort or intelligence. They're failures of isolation.
Here's what nobody says: The career ladder didn't disappear. It was pulled up. And millions of people—solo consultants, first-time founders, people who never planned to be entrepreneurs—are now building in mid-air.
They're told to "move fast and break things."
But when you're building alone, breaking things means breaking yourself.
We're entering an era where technology's job isn't to make us faster. It's to make us less alone in the decisions that matter.
Not AI that writes your emails. AI that pressure-tests your pricing before you send the proposal.
Not tools that automate tasks. Tools that act as the second opinion you don't have access to.
The question isn't whether independent work is the future. It's already here.
The question is whether the people building alone have the same probability of success as the people building with infrastructure, advisors, and safety nets.
Right now, they don't.
We're working to change that.
If you're building something alone right now—a practice, a product, a business you never imagined starting—you're not imagining the risk. It's real.
But so is the possibility that you don't have to do it blind.

You can use ChatGPT every day and still not understand what is happening under the hood.
That gap is where most mistakes get made.
These concepts are not just for developers. If you are using, managing, or making decisions about it, you should know them.
1. Context Window: Everything ChatGPT can "see" in a conversation. Information outside it does not exist for the model.
2. System Prompt: Hidden instructions set before the chat begins. This is how businesses customize ChatGPT's behavior and persona.
3. Token: The unit ChatGPT uses to read and write. Speed, cost, and limits are all measured in tokens, not words.
4. Temperature Controls: how predictable or creative the output is. Low temperature for accuracy. High temperature for brainstorming.
5. Prompt Engineering: Designing inputs that consistently produce useful outputs. Less art, more structure.
6. Few-Shot Prompting: Giving ChatGPT examples inside your prompt so it learns what you want by pattern, not description.
7. Chain-of-Thought: Asking ChatGPT to reason step by step before answering. Significantly improves accuracy on complex tasks.
8. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): Pulling in external data at runtime and feeding it into the model. This is how ChatGPT gets access to your documents and live information.
9. Hallucination: Confident, fluent, and wrong. The core risk to design around in any real workflow.
10. Agentic Mode: ChatGPT reasons, takes an action, observes the result, and repeats. It stops generating text and starts completing tasks.
Understanding these does not make you a developer. It makes you someone who can use, evaluate, and direct AI effectively.
Take one concept at a time. Go one level deeper each week.

I read a post here, where someone complained about asking a colleague a question and receiving a copy-pasted response straight from ChatGPT. The poster obviously recognized exactly where this came from, and deeply disliked the realization.
This is what happens when we optimize for speed over connection.
Businesses are losing the ability to talk to each other, because AI makes it easier not to. Someone asks you a question and instead of really pausing to consider it and think through your answer, you copy-paste. You let the tool do the work you should be doing. You've outsource your entire mind, when the human factor is *everything*.
I use artificial intelligence, and I'm doing my best to find the way to preserve myself inside of it. But there's a line.
What are you avoiding by letting AI answer for you?
If you're ready to confront it, along with your team, I lead groups of all kinds through the most human-centric circle I can. Phones tucked away, no recording allowed.
We speak out loud and in front of others, on a level where the human matters more than the title, where truth can't be masked for long, and we get to really lean into the energetic magic of many people gathering together for a shared purpose.

Ep.17: A New Approach to Problem-Solving: Michael Hyatt’s Coaching Method | upcoach
Listen in as we discuss the art of coaching with Michael Hyatt, who shares his belief that coaching is the single biggest point of leverage in business. Michael is the Founder and Chairman of Full Focus. He has scaled multiple companies over the years, including a $250M publishing company with 700+ employees and his own goal-achievement company.
Under his leadership, Full Focus has been featured in the Inc. 5000 list of the fastest-growing companies in America and Inc.’s Best Work Places list. He is also the author of several New York Times, Wall Street Journal, and USA Today bestselling books, including Your Best Year Ever, Free to Focus, Win at Work and Succeed at Life, and Mind Your Mindset. He has been married for over 45 years to his wife Gail, has five daughters, and ten grandchildren.
In this episode, Michael talks about the importance of customization in coaching and shares how asking the right question at the right time can completely shift the client’s perspective and lead to significant results.
A powerful example of this is his own experience with an executive coach, who asked him a critical question that forever changed his approach to leadership. Michael also touches on the power of the right question and shares a key question he asks his clients.
In the second part of our chat, Michael discusses how to build listening skills and shares his thoughts on using both indirect and direct coaching methods. He emphasizes the importance of lending perspective to clients to encourage them to take on their problems and make them more solvable. He also provides an example of how ‘chunking’ a problem can reduce its drama and make it more manageable.
Michael shares his approach to challenging his clients and reveals that he views his clients as big and strong, not small and fragile, and believes that it’s his role to stand for their greatness. Tune in to hear more of Michael’s insights and get a bonus tip on the power of asking the right questions.
Episode quotes
Coaching is the single biggest point of leverage in his business
Well, I’ve been a consumer of coaching for about 20 years, and I’ve never not had a coach during that time. I feel like coaching has been the single biggest point of leverage in my business, and the way I look at it, if you want to go further faster, get a coach because the slow, dumb way is to figure it all out yourself. I love having somebody that’s there as an advocate for me.
I couldn’t get that from my board when I was back in a corporate responsibility. You can’t get it even from your friends or your colleagues, but a coach that knows you that intimately and is acquainted with your business, I think, is a game changer.
Why you can’t get coaching from YouTube videos
It’s got to be customized. You know, every client’s situation is unique, and I think the right word at the right time, the right question at the right time, can make a huge difference, can shift everything for that person, and it certainly has for me.
The thing that’s made a big impact on the results of his clients
I really believe that thinking is where it starts. Thinking leads to the actions you take. The actions you take deliver the results. And if you want to change the results, you’ve got to swim upstream to get to the thinking. But how do you get access to the thinking? I’m not a mind reader.
Well, I realized that language is the key. The words people use reveal their thinking, and sometimes, just a subtle shift in the language can change everything for the client.
On clarifying problems before offering solutions
I want to make sure I understand the problem, and I’m not trying to fix the wrong problem. I think it’s important for people to be heard. And a lot of times, once people can externalize it, they see the problem with it as soon as they get it out. It’s just when it’s this ambiguous mess in their head that it feels unsolvable. But once they get it out, they often come to their own solutions.
Sometimes, you just have to listen and hear it out and make sure that you’re not jumping to a conclusion that’s not warranted.
As a coach, I’ve really had to develop my listening skills. And that doesn’t mean that I sometimes believe in directive coaching. I don’t like the model where it’s all indirect.
So, that’s definitely a tool in the toolbox, but I think once you get it, I think that’s the point where you can just apply the right tool in the right situation and make a difference. And sometimes you have to speak into that, but you’ve got to solve the right problem.

Justin H. and Kyle DuPont just hosted another incredible AI roundtable, absolutely organized, curated, and informative. What I like the most about this roundtable? This is the type of roundtable that stimulates new ways of thinking ~ 🧠
This very unique AI roundtable taking on the consultative approach guides the data executives/leaders to come to a conclusion, not told a conclusion. Here is my takeaway:
1) Pain points are shared across industries because moving from AI experimentation to production takes operational and pragmatic ways of thinking.
2) Different perspectives prevail around if AI truly brings "value". The first step that is missing is how we define value. AI ROI is absolutely needed, but what else?
3) AI investment is under the scrutiny. The opportunity is for those who can build a compelling narrative, zoom in/out while building the business planning, and strengthen cross-functional executive/leadership partnership.
There are more challenges than ever before when everything is moving at machine speed. The success belongs to those who persist and continue to learn and grow.

It emerged from the uncertainty and setbacks of CosBE’s early years—and from what we learned by working directly with SME leaders on real transformation challenges.

• Issue-First
• Lean and Agile
• Micro-AI Swarms

AI transformation should not begin with technology. It should begin with the unique value a company creates and the management issue that matters most.

— Workwolf is a recruitment services company that combines human recruiters with proprietary AI and psychometric technology to deliver predictive hiring intelligence at disruptive pricing. The company addresses a fundamental inefficiency in the $150B+ recruitment industry: traditional agencies charge 15-25% of candidate salary for subjectiveassessments with no performance accountability. Workwolf’s technology-enabled model delivers measurable quality improvements at significantly lower cost per hire. The proprietary technology platform includes two core components: Smart Resume Screening for contextual qualification matching, and Packfinder™ psychometrics for role-specific performance prediction. Unlike generic assessment tools, Packfinder™ models are calibrated using client performance data, creating organization-specific predictions that improve with scale. The business model starts at fees as low as 4% of annual salary for high-volume roles, rather than percentage-based fees of 15-25%, creating favorable unit economics for high-volume clients while maintaining strong margins through technology leverage. Target customers are mid-market companies with consistent hiring volume (2+ hires/month) across multiple locations—particularly retail, hospitality, healthcare, logistics, and call centers. These segments offer predictable demand and benefit most from Workwolf’s pattern recognition capabilities across distributed operations. Show Notes
Serial tech entrepreneurs who have built successful companies time and again have deep knowledge and expertise. When you can get them to open up and reveal their secrets to success it’s a great opportunity to learn. In this episode, Ben Wilde interviews Michael Hyatt, the founder of BlueCat Networks and Dyadem, as well as a well-known investor and speaker, and one of the hosts of the TV show Dragon’s Den. Find out what it takes to succeed in today’s cut-throat tech world. You'll hear about: -Working on your strengths and partnering for your weaknesses (3:35) -The importance of hiring big egos and letting your people make decisions (4:20) -Why autonomy and purpose are the keys to retaining top talent (6:48) -How to hire the right people (8:13) -Why tech companies need to be able to pivot (10:35) -The characteristics of great board members (13:04) -Some of Michael's biggest missteps and lessons learned (15:57) -The difference between good and great products (19:06) -The importance of security as a fundamental product feature (21:28) -Emerging opportunities in the life sciences(22:52) -Why you should and shouldn’t be worried about technology (26:13) -Why humans are bad at predicting the future (29:20) -The massive opportunities yet to emerge online (31:16)

CEOs Must Orchestrate Health Like Athletes Do
This title was summarized by AI from the post below.
Michael Hyatt
4mo
Report this post
𝗖𝗘𝗢𝘀 𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝗔𝘁𝗵𝗹𝗲𝘁𝗲𝘀. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗛𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵.
Professional athletes orchestrate their health with precision. Trainers, nutritionists, sleep coaches, recovery specialists, sports psychologists. Every data point is measured. Every pattern is reviewed.
Now consider the typical CEO.
Fragmented care across disconnected specialists. Annual physical. Quarterly therapy. Periodic spiritual reflection. No synthesis across domains. No one asking how the body, the mind, and the spirit are interacting.
For executives running multi-million dollar businesses, this is strategic malpractice. Your company depends on your capacity. Your capacity depends on every dimension working together.
I realized this after three ER visits in two years for what turned out to be acid reflux and stress. A top cardiologist told me my body, my mind, and my spirit were one system and that no single professional could see all of it at once.
That was twenty years ago. Last year I finally built the orchestrator I needed.
A Claude project loaded with my medical history, blood labs, genomic data, books I trust, and a structured instruction set. It doesn't replace my physicians, my therapist, or my spiritual director. It prepares me for every one of them. Synthesizes across all of them. Surfaces patterns that no individual specialist sees.
Three moves any CEO can make this quarter:
1. Build a self-care project and load your current health data.
2. Run preliminary analyses to prepare for every appointment.
3. Use it between appointments as a thinking partner across all three domains.
The executives who do this will pull ahead of the ones who don't.

My husband Stephen Hooper has been a physiotherapist for over two decades. And when I ask him what frustrates him most about the current healthcare system, his answer is always the same.
It's not the complexity of what he sees. It's the fact that people arrive having spent significant money on imaging, specialists, and repeated treatment, and nowhere along the way has anyone had an honest conversation with them.
Nobody has said: "Your lifestyle is not supporting your ability to heal."
Sleep deprivation, chronic stress, poor nutrition, insufficient movement; none of these show up on a scan. But all of them directly impact how the body responds to injury, manages pain, and recovers over time.
The result is that people keep seeking the next treatment, the next referral, the next answer... when the most important variables are the ones happening between appointments.
This is the conversation we prioritise at Effortless Superhuman. Not because it's easy to hear, but because it's the one that actually changes outcomes. Real clinical results come when treatment is paired with the conditions that allow the body to do what it's designed to do — heal.
If you work in health, allied health, or lead a team of people carrying significant physical and mental load, this conversation matters more than we're currently having it.
I'd be curious: in your experience, how often does lifestyle actually come up in a clinical or workplace health context?

The thing that makes you a great doctor might also be burning you out.
A 2022 study in BMC Health Services Research found that high self-critical perfectionism uniquely predicted both emotional exhaustion and depersonalization in physicians — two of the three core dimensions of burnout.
42% of physicians in the study met criteria for high emotional exhaustion or depersonalization burnout.
42%.
Let that land for a moment.
We were trained to get it right. Every time. No margin for error. A missed diagnosis isn't just a mistake — it's a moral failure. And so we internalized a standard that no human being can sustainably meet.
The same trait that drives us to study longer, document better, and advocate harder for our patients... is the same trait quietly accelerating our collapse.
This is not a character flaw. It's a training-induced wound.
The question isn't whether you're a perfectionist. Most of us are. The question is: Is your perfectionism working for you, or against you?
In Positive Intelligence terms, the inner critic driving perfectionism is called the Hyper-Achiever — the voice that says your worth is tied to your performance. It protects you from failure, but it never lets you rest. And it doesn't just drain you. It disconnects you from your patients, your colleagues, your family, and yourself. That's depersonalization. That's what the data shows.
Here's what I've learned coaching physicians:
You can hold high standards without letting them hold you hostage.
You can be excellent without being relentless.
You can care deeply without abandoning yourself in the process.
The system rewards your perfectionism. Your body is paying the bill.
If this resonates — I'd love to hear how perfectionism shows up in your practice. Drop it in the comments. You're not alone in this.

Reference: Kain ZN et al. "Perfectionism as a predictor of physician burnout." BMC Health Services Research, 2022. DOI: 10.1186/s12913-022-08785-7

In this photo, you see Tara Botarelli, who believed in the potential of this program 15 years ago, and David Kline, a graduate of the program, kicking off the latest cohort of future leaders in the company. As a bonus, we got to see Zack and Ray, who we trained as new hires just 3 years ago.
This is what great looks like. Develop early, develop often, take chances on people, and give them the opportunity to prove you right.
Congrats to the 11 members of this FOL class, congrats to Thermo IDD for continuing to drive leadership, and thanks so much for letting Applied Leadership Partners be a small part of this wonderful program. See you soon!

IP Address Management (IPAM)
March 30, 2011
Views: 12,125
BlueCat Networks, the IPAM Intelligence™ company with over 1,500 clients worldwide, has received the highest rating given to vendors in the Gartner authoritative “MarketScope for DNS, DHCP and IP Address Management (IPAM), 2011”* report.
In the MarketScope report, Lawrence Orans, a research director in Gartner’s Research organization, notes that “IPAM applications offer a range of capabilities for controlling, automating and managing the domain name and address space, and these tools are a significant improvement over spreadsheets and homegrown address management applications.” Further, “Gartner estimates that the DDI market generated approximately $216 million in 2010, representing a 23% increase over 2009. They estimate that the market will grow another 28% in 2011, to approximately $276 million.”
“We are thrilled to receive this ‘strong positive’ rating from Gartner based on an expert evaluation of our IP Address Management, DNS and DHCP solutions,” said Michael Hyatt, CEO and co-founder of BlueCat Networks. “We believe our momentum is unmatched in this report and it is proof that the investments we have made in our products and in our world-class support and professional services organizations are exactly what the market wants. BlueCat Networks’ success in winning several large deals, along with its strengthened distribution channel and solid organic growth, are powerful testaments to our product and business strategy.” Hyatt continued, “The proliferation of IP-enabled devices, as well as strategic initiatives such as virtualization and private clouds, are driving the adoption of IPAM solutions. BlueCat Networks is uniquely positioned to help organizations improve the manageability, resiliency and efficiency of their networks and, as a result, we are showing up on more ‘short lists’ of Gartner clients.”
To pre-order a complimentary copy of the Gartner MarketScope report, please visit: www.bluecatnetworks.com/gartner.

From Roommates to Co-Founders: The Story of Building & Selling a Successful Toronto-Based Tech Company — Sampford Advisors - Expert Tech M&A Advisor (Software, IT Services, SaaS, Hardware)
From Roommates to Co-Founders: The Story of Building & Selling a Successful Toronto-Based Tech Company
Let’s rewind all the way back to 1997. Two guys just enrolled at the University of Waterloo to study Computer Science. They became roommates. What eventually took place is a series of exciting and challenging moments, cool experiences, and invaluable lessons that anyone can learn from. Below is the story of Ravin Shah and Tishan Mills and their successful start-up QuickTapSurvey.
Ravin and Tishan graduated in 2002, shortly after the dot-com bubble had burst. Given the volatility in the economy, most people in their cohort took shelter in secure jobs with stable companies. For Ravin and Tishan, the excitement of starting something on their own took precedent, but getting to that point took some time, and some trial and error.
Ravin moved to Chicago and started working as a consultant for Accenture. He then worked for Lehman Brothers for a year before coming back to Toronto. Tishan did his Masters of Applied Science after finishing his bachelors and then worked for companies like IBM, Sapient, and RBC in their technology divisions.
They were always entrepreneurs at heart, but were just waiting for the right idea and the right time.
In 2009-2010 both Ravin and Tishan began seriously exploring the possibility of starting something. The mobile revolution was taking off, specifically with the introduction of the iPhone and later the tablet. And then, there was a defining moment. One day, as Ravin and Tishan were walking down the street, they were stopped by someone holding a clipboard asking if they could be surveyed on a topic. Noticing the hassle of using a paper-based technique was the tipping point both of them needed to ignite the spark of creativity. This exact moment gave birth to TabbleDabble (aka QuickTapSurvey).
--
To uncover the story of QuickTapSurvey, I sat down with Ravin and Tishan to learn about how they met, why they started the Company, what they did to grow the business, and their eventual decision to sell/exit.
Making it through the Valley of the Shadow
Reid Hoffman, internet entrepreneur, venture capitalist, and author (Co-Founder of LinkedIn) said “entrepreneurs can have, as part of their plan, the desire to become famous, cool or rich, but they do have to be driven by something more. 99.99% of all startups go through a Valley of the Shadow – where they think why did we think this was a good idea? Why did we think this was going to work?”
[George]: Did you go through the shadow?
[Ravin/Tishan]: Oh yeah. We felt that shadow every month for the first year! It was a deep shadow and even though you see the light, it’s definitely difficult for start-ups to get over that hump – especially ones that are bootstrapped. Funding was much more difficult to secure 8 years ago than it is now so not only did we have to get over that shadow, we had to do it in a very resourceful way.
[George]: What was the most difficult part of that experience?
[Tishan]: What made it difficult was the fact that we were investing our own money into this company, our own savings. On top of that, we were both not getting a salary in the first 2 years. To make things more interesting, my son Nathan was born – so I had a child, a mortgage, a family, and being an entrepreneur didn’t make it comforting at first. That was my personal shadow.
[George]: So what made you stick with it?
[Ravin]: Optimism. Time isn’t on your side when you’re building a business from scratch, so we had to keep pushing it on and what made a difference for us were small wins. During the journey, we had small wins that would provide the necessary motivation and money to unlock the next month…a few of those happened in succession to buy us enough time to stick with it.
[Tishan]: The other thing that was challenging is when we launched our product in 2012, we had little revenues at first, but the ball started rolling from there – we thought we’ll get to the 2014 mark in the first year so our expectations were off in terms of what it actually takes to grow a business.
Having the right partner(s) can make or break your success
According to Steve Hogan, Managing Director at Tech-RX (a Silicon-Valley based venture capital firm), the #1 thing failed start-ups have in common is that sole founders don’t have partners. Contrary to the popular misconception that entrepreneurship is a lonely road, a crucial factor to start-up success is aligning yourself with an all-star team that complement the gaps you have.
[George]: What roles did you take on in the beginning and how did you split them amongst yourselves?
[Ravin]: I was definitely more geared towards the sales and marketing aspect of the business – anything to do with client success. That being said, I didn’t really know the “sales process” that well either – things like following up, knowing your buyer, having a call to action, etc. weren’t as intuitive so I ended up spending lots of energy in the beginning doing things that were less effective.
[Tishan]: I guess we figured it out over time. It’s funny though because in the beginning, we would explain the business to a VC and they would be a little weary of our team as they would think Ravin and I were both computer science guys leading the management team. Eventually, we both fell into roles we naturally gravitated towards – Ravin was sales, marketing, customer experience and I was technology, product development, engineering, QA, etc.
[George]: What do you like most about having a Co-Founder?
[Ravin]: You can have vacations. No, seriously – it makes a huge difference to have someone as your backup, someone you can trust and is fully capable of running the business while you’re not there.
[Tishan]: It also helps to have someone who understands what you’re going through. That moral support is a big factor because as we’ve said before, when you’re going through that valley of the shadow and everything’s on the line, you can have that partner/friend to talk to and lift you up again.
[Ravin]: Also, even though we were friends, we still set formal rules and standards from the beginning. We even went as far as setting how many vacation days we can each take and that meant holding ourselves accountable to a company we had to grow/scale. Those conversations were awkward at first, especially because we were friends, but it’s better to have them upfront in the beginning to lay out what’s acceptable and what’s not.
[George]: When did you start feeling reassured about the success of the company?
[Ravin]: When we started paying ourselves a salary. When Tishan and I started working on QuickTapSurvey full time, we had no other choice but to make it a success – financially. Again, because we were bootstrapped, we had to think about profit from day one and it was a continuous process for us where the more we made, the more we would reinvest in the business.
[Tishan]: We moved into a tiny one-room office in Scarborough and as the company grew, we just started growing the space as well (expanding into other rooms within the building). Once the company started making real revenues, we not only grew in office space but in size of the team as well – that was super important to us as Co-Founders because we were essentially the ‘Chief Everything Officers’ for a long time.
Knowing when it’s the right time to do the right thing
Michael Hyatt, Co-Founder of BlueCat (which was sold for $400 million to a US firm) said that “entrepreneurs should be thinking about building a great business, and exits come from companies who run great businesses.”
[George]: At what point did selling the business become a consideration?
[Ravin]: We had calls showing interest in the company at many points of the journey, but we ignored most of them. Then, at one point, we started getting more calls and there seemed to be a larger interest in the market – seeing as though the market was hot and buyers were on the lookout we started to pay more attention to a potential exit.
[Tishan]: We were also product-focused tech founders who scaled the company to a certain level, and to take it to the next jump required different skillsets. At the point where we started thinking about a sale, we also had different options on the table like continuing to grow the business, but we figured that doing so would also mean absorbing more risk – and our families deserved some security.
[George]: What was the feeling like when you closed the sale?
[Ravin]: Sense of relief. It’s really an emotional rollercoaster when you’re going through the process because there are a lot of unknowns – being unsure of whether it’s going to work or not, going through the due diligence, the negotiations, etc.
[Tishan]: Once the pen touched the paper to sign/close, there was a sigh of relief – the goal was accomplished.
[George]: What are you looking forward to most now that it’s done?
[Tishan]: Definitely advising/mentoring some companies, and maybe starting another company sometime in the near future.
[Ravin]: Spending time with family, taking some time off, and getting recharged for the next venture!
[Ravin/Tishan]: All in all, its really been a fun ride, we learned so much through this process, and experienced a ton.
Key Takeaways
Expect the Valley of the Shadow - growing your business will be more challenging than you think
Stay optimistic and focus on small wins - A positive attitude and early success will allow you to stick with it longer
Profit is King - working on your bootstrapped start-up full-time, making a profit is a priority from day one
The “Foundation” Team - Find the right partner you can trust, and who has skillsets that complement your gaps
Build it RIGHT and they will Come - Focus on building a successful business first, and a successful exit will follow as a result

About Event
​Canada is at an inflection point. In this private session, join Michael Hyatt (DataStealth) and Dan Debow (Build Canada) for a candid conversation about how today's founders and operators can build, hire, invest in, and find their edge in Canada.
Important Note: This event is by invite only. You will be required to share more information about yourself in order to be accepted to join the event. Only those who receive approval will be admitted on the day of the event.
We are officially part of Toronto Tech Week 2025, a weeklong citywide collection of events to connect and celebrate the builders. June 23 → June 27, 2025 | torontotechweek.com.
​About our Speakers:
​Michael Hyatt is a serial entrepreneur and investor. He co-founded BlueCat, which was acquired by Madison Dearborn Partners in Chicago, IL, and Dyadem, acquired by IHS (NYSE: IHS). Presently, Michael serves as a Senior Advisor at Northleaf Capital Partners and shares his business insights as a commentator on CBC. Michael was also a Founding Partner at the prestigious Creative Destruction Lab (CDL) within the Rotman School of Management.
Michael holds the role of Executive Chairman at DataStealth.io, an enterprise cybersecurity firm that allows organizations to discover, classify, and protect their most sensitive data and documents, ensuring that sensitive data and documents are secure and that they meet applicable privacy, regulatory, governance and compliance requirements.
Beyond business, Michael is active in philanthropy, leading the Hyatt Family Foundation. The foundation's primary areas of focus encompass women's health, critical hospital research, and support for underprivileged minorities.
​Daniel Debow is a Founding Member of Build Canada and a former VP of Partnerships and Corporate Development at Shopify.
Daniel was previously CEO and founder of Helpful, a startup backed by Bessemer Ventures that was acquired by Shopify in 2019. Prior to that, Daniel was SVP, Emerging Technologies at Salesforce and co-founded Rypple, which was acquired by Salesforce in 2011. Prior to Rypple, Daniel was VP Marketing & Corp Dev for Workbrain, which was acquired by Infor in 2007.
​Daniel is an early investor in over 50 technology companies. In 2015 he was recognized as Canada’s “Angel Investor of the Year”. Daniel holds a JD/MBA (Gold Medalist) from the University of Toronto, an LLM from Stanford University and a BA (Psych) from Western University.

At Full Focus, we were spending $33,000/month on a fractional CFO and outsourced accounting—$396,000 annually.
The output was adequate. Standard reports. Monthly reviews. Nothing that gave us real-time strategic visibility.
We made a structural change: an AI architect and controller support at $15,000/month ($180,000/year). The architect built a complete system of AI agents and automated processes—including deep financial analysis capabilities we never had with traditional accounting.
The result: $216,000 in annual savings with measurably superior output.
This isn’t an argument for eliminating finance roles. It’s an argument for rethinking how financial intelligence gets delivered in a mid-market business. AI didn’t just cut costs—it created capabilities that didn’t previously exist at our scale.
Every business has at least one function where AI can deliver this kind of structural improvement. The challenge is identifying it, designing the right solution, and managing the transition.
That’s precisely the work we do inside the AI Business Lab Mastermind—a curated group of $1M+ business owners implementing AI together through in-person intensives, monthly working sessions, and ongoing peer collaboration.
A handful of spots remain.

🚨 AI in Finance: Hype vs Reality — What 25 CFOs Told Us
On 24th March, 25 CFOs, Finance Directors, Controllers, and AI innovators joined an exclusive AI for CFOs | VIP London Event | Driving 35% Operational Efficiency Event - and the insights were refreshingly honest.
Here’s what stood out from our live poll 👇
📊 State of AI adoption is still early
• 42% — No adoption
• 42% — Still in pilot stage
• 0% — Fully integrated across finance
→ AI in finance isn’t a maturity story yet - it’s still an exploration phase
📊 Clarity gap is real
Only a small group fully understands where AI can add value — most are still figuring it out
📊 Biggest barriers? Not what you think
• Lack of internal AI skills (top challenge)
• Data quality & availability issues
• Legacy systems & integration complexity
→ Interestingly, cost and vendor selection were barely concerns
📊 Why invest in AI?
• #1 driver: Operational Efficiency
• Followed by: Better decision-making & competitive advantage
📊 What’s next?
Most expect 10–60% of finance workflows to be AI-enabled within 2 years - a strong signal that change is coming fast
💡 What we explored together
We moved beyond theory into real, applied use cases:
• Agentic AI for Invoice Processing (with SAP integration)
• Agentic AI for VAT Verification
• How CFO teams can get started with Anthropic Claude skills
🤔 The questions that mattered most
The discussion was incredibly practical and grounded:
• “How do we trust outputs and manage hallucinations?”
• “What governance frameworks ensure safety?”
• “If our data isn’t clean, should we even start?”
• “What happens to today’s AI solutions when models rapidly improve?”
→ The takeaway: AI success in finance isn’t just about technology — it’s about trust, data, and adaptability.
🔑 Final reflection
Finance leaders aren’t resisting AI — they’re rightfully cautious.
But the shift from pilots to production will come down to clear use cases, strong data foundations, and controlled experimentation.

The real value of AI lies not just in automation, but in augmenting decision-making, improving accuracy, and unlocking forward-looking insights that were previously difficult to achieve.

AI enables more accurate and dynamic forecasting by analysing historical data and external variables, allowing finance teams to anticipate risks and opportunities proactively.
𝙍𝙚𝙖𝙡-𝙏𝙞𝙢𝙚 𝙄𝙣𝙨𝙞𝙜𝙝𝙩𝙨 & 𝘿𝙚𝙘𝙞𝙨𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙎𝙪𝙥𝙥𝙤𝙧𝙩
With AI-driven dashboards and analytics, leadership can access real-time financial and operational insights, enabling faster and more informed decisions.
𝘼𝙪𝙩𝙤𝙢𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙤𝙛 𝙍𝙤𝙪𝙩𝙞𝙣𝙚 𝙋𝙧𝙤𝙘𝙚𝙨𝙨𝙚𝙨

AI significantly reduces manual intervention, improving data integrity, consistency, and reliability across financial systems.

AI helps identify inefficiencies, spending patterns, and cost drivers, enabling organisations to optimise costs without compromising growth.

🔹 From use cases to transformation

Upskilling, change leadership, and governance are no longer “soft topics” — they are core enablers of value and trust, and they are being addressed alongside technology in real implementations.

AI in Finance: Where CFOs Actually See ROI
When AI is discussed in finance, the conversation often jumps to big promises.
But most CFOs look at it differently.
The real question is simple:
Does it solve real operational problems and deliver measurable ROI?
In many finance departments today, a large portion of time is still spent on activities such as:
• Verifying and validating invoice data
• Cross-checking invoices with purchase orders and receipts
• Investigating mismatches and duplicate transactions
• Correcting manual entry errors
• Following up for approvals
• Reconciling financial records across systems
These tasks are necessary, but they create operational bottlenecks, delays, and hidden costs.
This is where AI applied to real finance workflows makes a difference.
In practical use cases, AI helps by:
• Automatically capturing and interpreting financial documents
• Performing invoice verification and validation with rule-based and AI checks
• Identifying mismatches, duplicates, and anomalies early
• Routing approvals through structured workflows
• Providing clearer visibility into financial transactions and liabilities
For CFOs, the value is not theoretical.
It shows up in measurable outcomes such as:
✔ Reduced manual processing effort
✔ Lower error and correction rates
✔ Faster financial processing cycles
✔ Better financial visibility for decision-making
AI in finance does not eliminate the need for finance professionals.
Instead, it reduces repetitive rework and allows finance teams to focus on analysis, controls, and strategic financial management.
The real value of AI in finance is not hype.
It is solving real operational problems and improving how finance functions operate every day.

Summary
Michael Hyatt, productivity expert and author of Free to Focus and Your Best Year Ever, discusses how to achieve success at work while maintaining a fulfilling personal life. He shares his transformational journey from working 15-hour days as a division manager to implementing boundaries that enabled him to win in both professional and personal domains, introducing the concept of the Full Focus Planner as a practical tool for managing nine life domains.
Insights
Productivity gains plateau after 50 hours of work per week; beyond this threshold, output becomes counterproductive due to fatigue and diminished cognitive function
Creating hard boundaries around work (specific start/stop times) paradoxically increases productivity by forcing innovation and eliminating distractions within constrained timeframes
The messy middle—where initial enthusiasm fades and results aren't yet visible—is where most meaningful goals fail; reconnecting with your 'why' is essential to persevere
Resources are never the limiting factor in achieving goals; lack of resources forces the human creativity and innovation that actually drives success
Saying 'no' clearly and kindly using the 'yes-no-yes' framework (acknowledge, decline due to commitments, offer alternative help) builds respect rather than resentment
Trends
Holistic life management frameworks gaining traction as professionals seek balance across multiple life domains beyond careerBoundary-setting and time-blocking becoming recognized productivity strategies rather than work-life balance luxuriesShift from goal-setting to goal-achievement focus, emphasizing execution and persistence over initial planningIncreased demand for physical planners and analog tools as counterbalance to digital distraction and screen fatigueIntegration of family and business succession planning, with next-generation leaders (like Joel Miller and Megan Hyatt) taking operational rolesCoaching and executive mentorship becoming mainstream professional development rather than outlier practiceSpontaneity and white space in calendars being recognized as essential for creativity and family connectionNine-domain life assessment models (body, mind, spirit, love, family, community, money, work, hobbies) becoming standard personal development framework

The biggest lesson this week wasn't about AI.
Three years ago, I thought better technology solved operational problems.
After working across manufacturing, hospitality, HR systems, analytics, and now building Precision Pulse, I've realised something different.
Technology rarely fixes confusion.
It simply scales it.

That's one pattern I've started calling Decision Friction.
When decisions aren't clearly defined, every new system inherits the confusion.

Understand the process.
Understand the people.

Another pattern from client conversations this year about productivity with AI.
Ask individuals, and AI is clearly working. The deck that took two days or more takes two hours. The analysis that used to take three days goes out the same day. Nobody's making this up.
Ask the organization, and the story dissolves. Productivity metrics are flat. No one can point to ROI. Leaders can't even confirm output has gone up. They just know everyone says they're faster. One explanation is that people are overestimating their own gains. It's comforting for skeptics, but the faster turnarounds are real.
The explanation I've come to believe is this: the gains are real, and they're being spent before anyone counts them.
Software teams show the mechanics most clearly. Faros AI analyzed telemetry from more than 10,000 developers and found that teams with high AI adoption merged 98% more pull requests, while review time rose 91%. The developer finishes the feature in two days instead of five. Then the branch waits in a review queue that didn't get any faster ,and therefore the overall cycle time still stays or maginally reduces. Any surplus saving converts into more tests, more edge cases, better documentation. Delivery metrics, stay flat, while individual output climbs.
The same story repeats outside engineering. Saved time is not wasted. It becomes another revision round, a more tailored version, a rising standard where last year's above-and-beyond is this year's baseline. Therefore, nothing in the P&L moves.
Spending the gain isn't a failure. It might be the best available outcome, if the spend is directed. More tailoring for your top accounts is a strategy. More polish on internal decks is a leak. Right now, most organizations aren't able to tell those two apart.
Capacity, like any budget, gets allocated either by decision or by drift.

I put my entire company inside a cube.
Of course, the cube is fictional.
But the problem it represents is not.
Most growing businesses do not suffer from a lack of software. They suffer from a lack of connection.
Sales has its system.
Operations has another.
Finance maintains separate records.
Management follows up through messages, calls and meetings.
Technology keeps adding integrations to hold everything together.
Every department may be working—but the company is not operating as one system.
That is where AI and automation become genuinely valuable.
Not as another chatbot.
Not as another isolated dashboard.
But as an operating layer that connects information, identifies exceptions, coordinates action and gives leadership visibility across the business.
The goal is not to remove people from the company.
It is to remove the repetitive coordination that prevents capable people from doing their best work.

Most companies don’t have an urgency problem.
They have a visibility problem.
That’s why nothing moves.
Because urgency only exists when pain is visible.
And in most companies, it isn’t.
The real issues are buried inside:
Work that “kind of works” but drains time every day
Decisions slowed because no one sees the full picture
Teams manually compensating for broken processes
Small inefficiencies quietly compounding
No alarms.
No crisis.
No clear signal.
So leadership tells themselves:
“We’re fine. Maybe later.”
But here’s the trap:
👉 No visible chaos doesn’t mean things are under control
👉 It usually means problems are silently scaling
And this is exactly why most AI projects fail.
Companies try to automate…
something they don’t fully see.
So they end up:
Scaling confusion
Accelerating broken workflows
Adding tools on top of unclear operations
AI doesn’t fix visibility.
It amplifies whatever is already there.
The real question isn’t:
“Where can we use AI?”
It’s:
“Where are we already losing control… without seeing it?”
Because here’s the uncomfortable truth:
If you need a crisis to see the problem, you’re already late.
By the time it becomes visible,
you’re not fixing a problem anymore,
You’re dealing with a system
that’s already out of control.
Most companies don’t act too late because they’re careless.
They act too late because
by the time it’s undeniable… it’s already expensive.
If things feel “fine” but heavier than they should…
That’s not growth.
That’s operational drag compounding.

In my last post, I talked about how organizations move toward controlled autonomy at scale.
That only works if something does not automate.
Human judgment.
In the last cycle, we valued people for execution, how fast they could produce, analyze, and deliver.
AI is taking a significant portion of that execution. Not completely, but enough to change the equation.
So what remains valuable?
It comes down to a shift already happening.
From answers to questions.
From output to judgment.
From doing to deciding.
The paradox is already visible. More content, more analysis, more output, and less clarity.
This is where the role of the human changes.
Not as the executor of work, but as the curator of direction. The one who decides what gets attention, what gets built, and what gets ignored.
For the next generation, this is fundamental.
Competing on answers is no longer a strategy. AI has commoditized that.
Competing on judgment is.
Understanding what matters, why it matters, and when it does not.
For enterprises, this is strategic.
You can automate execution. You cannot outsource judgment.
The organizations that win will be the ones that elevate how their people think, not just how they produce. In a world of infinite output, value comes from what you choose not to do.
The question then becomes: how do you build systems that keep human judgment at the center as more execution is handled by systems?
That is the next problem to solve.

Most SME businesses don’t lose to technology.
They lose to what technology changes next.
I see a common pattern when working with business owners.
They look at new technology and ask:
“What does this do?”
That’s the wrong question.
The better question is:
“What will this change next?”
I use a simple framework with clients:
The Smith Second-Order Advantage™
1. SPOT – What’s emerging?
2. SHIFT – What will change?
3. STRESS – Where does this pressure your business?
4. SEIZE – Where is the opportunity?
A quick example (AI):
SPOT → AI tools improving admin
SHIFT → Customers expect faster responses
STRESS → Manual processes become too slow
SEIZE → Automate, respond quicker, win more work
Most businesses focus on step 1.
The advantage sits in steps 2, 3 and 4.
Technology doesn’t just improve businesses.
It quietly changes the rules of the game.
And by the time those rules are obvious…
your competitors are already playing differently.
Final thought:
Don’t just ask what’s changing.
Ask what that change will change next.

comment FRAMEWORK and I’ll send it over.
